players.product: frontier model training/inference on liquid-cooled GPU clusters wired with Credo 7-meter ZeroFlap AECs (Memphis)

quarterly_data.signal: Named by Credo's CEO as the customer that drove the ZeroFlap architecture. Building in another data center, xAI was struggling mightily with link flaps - connections that disconnect and reconnect, propagating bad data and forcing the cluster to be brought down and reset - and could not keep availability above even 90%. Moving into its own liquid-cooled data center with 'tons of power to the racks,' xAI asked Credo to extend its AEC family from 3 meters to 7 meters so that every connection in the row could be copper. Brennan visited Memphis over the summer: xAI has achieved 99.9% uptime and brings a cluster up in 5 days versus 6 to 8 weeks, which he frames as worth a billion-dollar increment of revenue for a month of compute.

quarterly_data.signal: Management: the semiconductor value chain is experiencing a major structural supply shift driven primarily by the AI data center boom, creating critical shortages in advanced packaging, specialized materials and memory allocation. Q2 inventory turnover days were 107 (105 in Q1); a meaningful portion of inventory remains in work in process mainly due to the constraint in available OSAT capacity, as industry-wide capacity continues to be prioritized for AI server demand. Realtek has qualified multiple vendors to diversify supply and applies 'design for availability' principles to reduce exposure to constrained materials; it views around 100 days of inventory as normal and healthy, and says IC inventory at distributors and direct customers remains healthy.

Very few, if any, products are likely to remain unaffected; product lines and magnitude were not disclosed (handled case by case). The memory price hike together with OSAT supply constraints has reached a level Realtek can no longer fully absorb on its own.

quarterly_data.signal: CALL — THE FIBER-CONTENT-PER-GPU FRAMEWORK (the definitive supply-side math for optical in AI factories). Base case: enterprise grows at the rate GPUs grow; THREE drivers add on top. (1) CLUSTER SIZE: clusters ABOVE ~130,000 GPUs exceed a 512-radix switch's two-layer span and need a THIRD OPTICAL LAYER -> ~50% MORE CONTENT PER GPU for very large clusters. (2) BANDWIDTH (doubles ~every 2 years): Hopper -> Blackwell kept 100G SerDes so fibers went 8 -> 16 per GPU (content DOUBLED); the RUBIN era jumps SerDes to 200G with lane count flat -> NEUTRAL; Feynman (~2029-30): fibers double again IF SerDes stays 200G, neutral if 400G arrives (BiDi/WDM could offset) — Springboard conservatively assumes NEUTRAL. (3) SCALE-UP, today 100% COPPER: Vera Rubin Ultra NVL576 is a HYBRID step — copper inside each 72-GPU rack, DIRECT OPTICAL rack-to-rack. Bracketing a full-optical scale-up: 14.4 Tbps scale-up / 200G = 72 lanes x 2 fibers = 144, plus scale-out 1.6 Tbps / 200G = 16 fibers -> 160 FIBERS PER GPU = 10x today's 16-fiber scale-out-only content (reality lands between; % of optical ports is confidential). COMBINED: optical content per GPU +1.3-1.5x BY 2028 and 'much, much higher' toward 2030. Status: Q2 enterprise strength is 'ALL JUST SCALE-OUT — we are not yet seeing scale-up or photonics in our results'; orders accelerating; 'if we could make more, we could sell more.'
quarterly_data.figure: Content/GPU drivers: 3rd optical layer >130k GPUs (+50%); Blackwell 16 fibers; full-optical scale-up = 160 fibers/GPU (10x); +1.3-1.5x by 2028

quarterly_data.signal: CALL — PHOTONICS: A $10B MAP BY 2030, AND THE LTA MODEL: Corning's new PHOTONICS Market-Access Platform targets $10 BILLION of revenue by 2030 — passive photonics INSIDE THE BOX (FAU harnesses and everything that moves/manages light between the faceplate and the silicon-photonics optical engine) for CPO/NPO, where Corning historically had ZERO content; likely starts with scale-out, and optical SCALE-UP supercharges it; the plan is built on 'assumptions and discussions AND AGREEMENTS with customers.' Despite industry chatter on scale-up timing, 'NO CHANGES to our fundamental belief... inside the real ecosystem there is much less drama than what it looks like from outside.' Business model: long-term agreements (Amazon multi-billion, NVIDIA, Meta up-to-$6B, Apple) will be 'the LION'S SHARE of our optical business' — every major capacity expansion is underpinned by risk/reward-sharing LTAs; profitability comes from innovation value-share, not bare-fiber pricing (optical NI +77% to a record 21% margin). Springboard math: run rate $20B by end-2026 (Q3 guide may hit it a QUARTER EARLY) -> $30B (2028) -> $40B (2030), 19% CAGR; high-confidence variant $27B/$35B; biggest risk-adjustment between the two = SCALE-UP TIMING. Elsewhere: memory prices push handsets down mid-teens % (Gorilla outperforms on content) but push TVs LARGER/premium (favors Gen 10.5); solar recovers from Q3 toward a $3B stream, with MORE POLYSILICON SHIFTING TO SEMICONDUCTOR (ELECTRONIC) GRADE at Hemlock; FY capex ~$2B.

quarterly_data.signal: New named customer announced the day before the conference: a multi-year, multi-billion-dollar deal with Verizon to help build out a new long-haul network that supports both Verizon's broadband business and data center interconnect. Corning has supplied Verizon for 30 years. Schlesinger grouped Verizon with the extended Lumen agreement and the previously announced Zayo agreement as the three deals now carrying the DCI business, and said the same fully connectorized solution logic applies to Verizon's fiber-to-the-home build.
quarterly_data.figure: multi-year, multi-billion-dollar deal with Verizon; 30 years as a Verizon supplier

quarterly_data.signal: Data center interconnect pulled forward: Corning had previously shared that DCI was about a $1 billion opportunity, $1 billion a year by the end of the decade. With the Lumen extension, the Zayo agreement and the new Verizon deal, management now expects to reach that number much sooner than the end of the decade and believes the opportunity is bigger than that, with an update to follow. Corning's dense fiber cables — more fibers in the same cable diameter — are the reason it is winning DCI, and are what it sells Lumen.
quarterly_data.figure: DCI $1 billion a year by the end of the decade now expected much sooner than the end of the decade and bigger than that

quarterly_data.signal: Quarter-to-date update, six weeks after the Q2 call: Corning expects to deliver the $20 billion annualized run rate a quarter early, in the third quarter, which puts sales at the high end or slightly better than the guidance given back in July. The third quarter is running really well and the fourth quarter is expected to be bigger than the third, with the high teens year-over-year growth seen in Q2 and Q3 continuing into Q4 and into next year. The $30 billion by end-2028 and $40 billion by end-2030 Springboard targets were explicitly NOT upgraded today, though management says deals like Verizon give more confidence in reaching the upper bound and maybe beyond.
quarterly_data.figure: $20 billion run rate a quarter early in Q3; sales at the high end or slightly better than July guidance; high teens YoY growth continuing into Q4 and next year; $30 billion / $40 billion targets unchanged

quarterly_data.signal: Capacity and constraints: Corning is not fiber constrained today but expects to be, which is why it committed to significantly increase US fiber capacity at what it calls the world's largest, lowest-cost fiber factory; that capacity starts coming online in the not that distant future and is tied to customer agreements. Cable and connectivity capacity has been added quarter over quarter for close to a year, and connectivity is where Corning expects to be most constrained relative to today's capacity as scale-up drives growth. Customers are funding part of the build through deposits they earn back by purchasing, and Corning modularises capacity adds rather than bringing on a whole factory at a time.
quarterly_data.figure: no specific figure

quarterly_data.signal: Photonics timing sharpened: Corning is planning to build out a $10 billion business by the end of the decade, from no sales today, selling into NPO and CPO applications inside the server tray, and is building out the supply chain now — hopefully next year we will start to see some sales there. The single biggest variable for the Springboard high-confidence gap is CPO adoption; the CPO supply chain at the scale required does not exist today and is the largest build investors should watch, though management sees no showstopper. Schlesinger expects the adoption inflection in the next four or five years rather than in 2027, with near-term content coming from traditional product sets (polarization-maintaining fiber, FAUs) and GlassBridge-type products a 2030-plus opportunity. Scale-up of the network should begin at the end of next year and run 2028 through 2030; today's growth is scale-out, where clusters above 130,000 GPUs add another network layer.
quarterly_data.figure: $10 billion photonics business by the end of the decade from no sales today; first sales hoped for next year; adoption inflection in the next four or five years, not 2027; 130,000 cluster barometer

Full year 2025: sales grew 13% to a record $16.4 billion, EPS grew 29% to $2.52, operating margin 19.3%, free cash flow $1.7 billion. CEO: enterprise was about $3 billion for the year, 'Roughly two-thirds of that would be the hyperscalers, of which Meta was one.' CFO: a little over $3 billion in enterprise; enterprise in total grew 60% and the hyperscale portion grew almost double that rate in 2025. Direct hyperscaler sales (such as Meta) are booked in enterprise; sales to carriers are booked in carrier.
quarterly_data.figure: enterprise +61% (FY2025); enterprise about $3 billion; roughly two-thirds hyperscalers; hyperscale portion grew almost double the enterprise rate

quarterly_data.signal: Carrier Networks grew 15% in full year 2025, primarily from sales to interconnect data centers. CFO: long-haul data center interconnect has so far gone through carriers ('our customers, for example, Lumen, are building out networks for data centers'), which sits in the carrier business. He expects carrier to grow over the next several years, with fiber-to-the-home also growing, but 'probably the largest driver is data center interconnect.'
quarterly_data.figure: carrier +15% (FY2025); majority of growth from data center interconnect

quarterly_data.signal: Supply/pricing color: CEO said that 'on a generic basis... there is enough fiber in the world to meet demand', but the capacity expansions are for Corning's new high-density fiber, cable and connectivity products, where demand is 'very, very robust' and 'If we could make more of these new products, we could sell more.' These products give customers better, more reliable optical performance 'in about half the space with significantly reduced installation cost'. He expects some of that value creation to end up accruing to shareholders as Corning begins to master manufacturing of these product sets, so profitability should improve over time. He added that the new products are increasing demand for Corning's products relative to others' products.
quarterly_data.figure: no specific figure

quarterly_data.signal: Hyperscaler long-term agreements beyond Meta: Corning is 'concluding similar long-term agreements with other major customers to dedicate capacity for them as well'. CEO: 'They are of a similar size and scale, each of them, to the Meta agreement', and there are 'several of them'. They are not yet fully included in the upgraded SpringBoard plan because not all have been concluded, and because the dedicated capacity is still being built, 'we won't see the financial impact really until you get into '27, and then it will continue to build to 2028.' The structures share cost and risk through customer prepayments and stringent long-term customer commitments, modelled on the display 'Gen ten and a half' agreements and Apple's $2.5 billion cover-glass commitment.
quarterly_data.figure: each similar in size and scale to the up to $6 billion Meta agreement; financial impact from '27, building to 2028

quarterly_data.signal: Scale-up optics timing (CEO, answering a CPO/scale-up question): 'we do not have a significant revenue amount for scale-up included in this most recent SpringBoard upgrade', so it would be on top. Photons use 'greater than three times lower power' than electrons even over very short links, and the advantage 'can be 20 times or more' at longer reach or higher bit rate. There is a broad effort to bring optics into scale-up, closer to the GPUs and switch ASICs; he believes those links going to photons, with Corning's innovations playing a significant role, is inevitable. On timing, some scenarios fall between now and 2028 and others start 'primarily starting immediately in 2028 and beyond', so the plan treats timing conservatively.

quarterly_data.signal: SpringBoard upgrade (first announced on this call): the internal plan now adds $11 billion in incremental annualized sales by 2028, up from the original $8 billion, taking the annualized run rate from $13.1 billion at the Q4 2023 start to $24 billion by 2028. For 2026, the internal plan now adds $6.5 billion (from $6 billion) and the high-confidence plan now adds $5.75 billion (from $4 billion). Corning has added $4.6 billion of incremental annualized sales since launch, hitting the upgraded high-confidence target a year early. quarterly_data.signal: LAUNCH (the release's key takeaway reads 'Launch of'): Corning Contour Form Micro Cable, part of the Corning GlassWorks AI Solutions portfolio, introduced at ECOC 2026. It is a high-density micro cable that increases fiber density in existing pathways, improves cable routing and supports fast air-assisted installation, optimized for metro and long-distance AI data center interconnects so operators can maximize pathway utilization and scale on existing infrastructure. Corning states it enables up to 50% more fiber in the same duct, for a step-reduction in duct size; it is built on Corning's Contour fiber for a compact footprint with installer-friendly handling.
quarterly_data.figure: up to 50% more fiber in the same duct

quarterly_data.signal: SHOWCASE (on display at ECOC, not described as a launch): Corning Multicore Fiber Solution, an integrated fiber, cable and connectivity offering that packs four cores into a single fiber strand, giving four times the capacity per fiber within the standard 125-micron cladding footprint for AI data center network density. Stated installation effects: up to 75% fewer connectors, which reduces cable mass by up to 70% and helps cut installation time by up to 60%.
quarterly_data.figure: four cores into a single fiber strand; four times the capacity per fiber within the standard 125-micron cladding footprint; up to 75% fewer connectors; reduces cable mass by up to 70%; cut installation time by up to 60%

quarterly_data.signal: SHOWCASE (on display at ECOC, not described as a launch): Corning MMC connector with PRIZM TMT ferrule technology, an expanded-beam ferrule that integrates precision-aligned microlenses into the MMC connector platform so optical signals pass through a contactless connection instead of traditional fiber-to-fiber physical contact. Corning states it reduces connection complexity versus physical-contact solutions, supports high-volume scalability and faster deployment, keeps performance consistent and is less sensitive to dust, debris and field-handling variability; it is designed to support insertion loss as low as 0.5 dB.
quarterly_data.figure: insertion loss as low as 0.5 dB

quarterly_data.signal: ON DISPLAY (the release calls it Corning's 'established' portfolio, not a launch): end-to-end passive Co-Packaged Optics (CPO) and Near-Packaged Optics (NPO) photonics connectivity solutions that bring fiber closer to the chip inside the data center (fiber-to-chip connectivity) for reliability, bandwidth density and energy efficiency in AI applications. Named components: detachable fiber-to-chip connectors, bend-resilient fibers optimized for CPO/NPO architectures, and pre-assembled passive optical management trays that simplify installation and enable scalable deployment.
quarterly_data.figure: no specific figure

quarterly_data.signal: SHOWCASE: scale-up cable management system, a data center rack demonstration of high-density optical connectivity handling the cable demands of next-generation servers, GPUs, LPUs and switches as vertical connections within the rack increase; the cable jumper system runs in a protective pathway to keep cables organized and unobstructed. The compact three-tray mini-rack also features a CPO-enabled optical backplane architecture, using light-based connections placed close to the chip.
quarterly_data.figure: no specific figure

quarterly_data.signal: Scope of the ECOC 2026 showing: the innovations belong to Corning's GlassWorks AI Solutions portfolio (a new micro cable, a multicore fiber solution, next-generation connectors, and co-packaged optics systems for scale-out of larger AI networks). Corning technology is featured in several joint demonstrations, including live showcases of multicore fiber solutions and co-packaged optics systems, and Corning technical experts give presentations on AI-optimized data center architecture and advanced co-packaged optics systems. Claude Echahamian (VP and GM, Emerging Businesses and EMEA, Corning Optical Communications) said AI is reshaping network requirements across Europe and beyond, and that Corning's portfolio spans advanced fiber technology, data center interconnects, subsea infrastructure and fiber-to-home broadband.
quarterly_data.figure: no specific figure

quarterly_data.signal: Corning's role in the Lumentum / Qualcomm Technologies / Corning joint ECOC 2026 demonstration (announced by Lumentum): a board-level, massively parallel optical die-to-die (D2D) interconnect for AI scale-up, designed for future CPO and NPO implementations and extending D2D connectivity over multimode fiber links spanning tens of meters. Corning's multimode fiber glass ferrules provide the high-density fiber connectivity used in the demonstration, which the release says highlights the importance of fiber density as optical links move closer to compute devices and advanced packaging environments. Claude Echahamian (VP and GM, Emerging Businesses and EMEA, Corning Optical Communications) said that as optical links move closer to compute devices, fiber connectivity must support increasing density, precision and scalability, and that Corning's multimode fiber solutions and MMC connectivity help enable the demonstration.
quarterly_data.figure: no specific figure

Lumentum remains confident in an ultra-high-power laser chip demand ramp in the second half of calendar 2027, ahead of customer scale-up deployments in calendar 2028. Because the first phase of scale-up optical connections spans across compute racks within a cluster, the ramp applies to any topology larger than one rack. The new 200G-per-lane CW laser chip has a significantly reduced die size, is more efficient, and delivers margins accretive to long-term financial targets; Lumentum is commanding a significant price premium versus market price because tight spec width produces superior transceiver yields at customers. The margin gap between CW and EML 'has closed considerably' since the prior call (EML still better). Better-than-expected output in Japan is being allocated to CW, and Lumentum is now shipping CW lasers in a relatively meaningful way into the 200G-per-lane silicon photonics opportunity, on top of internal deployment in its own transceivers.

Scale-across demand is being driven by inferencing and training applications requiring full-rate connectivity between data centers, plus political and regulatory constraints favoring smaller, more modular builds. Scale of the DCI opportunity: for one major hyperscaler, the network capacity connecting just two AI data center sites is double the total global backbone capacity that hyperscaler built over the entirety of the last decade.

We started with customers other than Google... we actually have customers that were much more substantial than Google in our early rounds of shipments.' One of the more interesting emerging use cases is deploying an OCS inside the rack itself, one per rack, to route around GPUs or TPUs that have failed or are overloaded - a surprising number of GPUs in a data center fail, and a compute model can represent '$20, 30, $40 million of compute time'. At the lead customer the number of OCSs per torus is also going up. As a result the $8 billion OCS TAM Lumentum published at OFC 'now looks like it's significantly under called', and a new, significantly higher TAM number is expected at the next OFC in March of next year. quarterly_data.signal: New EML economics and share math. Moving from 100G to 200G EML gives 'about a 2x uplift in price' - ASPs roughly double - and 200G lasers arrive at the 1.6T node. At 200G there is 'very little competition': Broadcom is a supplier of 200G EMLs, Lumentum is the other large supplier, and management sees no other entrants soon. On mix, EML-based transceivers are 'probably 70%-80%' of the 800G market but are expected to be only '40%-50% of the market at 1.6T' as silicon photonics takes share, so raw EML units go up while share comes down. At 3.2T Lumentum's transceiver engineers say 'silicon photonics again runs out of steam', producing 'a double whammy' where both EML unit numbers and EML share rise. Hurlston also framed the yield argument behind the price premium: the tolerance of the laser sets transceiver yield more than anything else, so a higher laser price 'more than makes up for itself in the high yields'.

At the 1.6T transition Lumentum got to the head of the curve on signal integrity and is 'now shipping ahead of great competitors like InnoLight and Coherent' (Eoptolink also named), first to market on a lot of its SKUs. The unresolved problem is gross margin - still below the top competitors - which management plans to attack on the manufacturing side entering calendar 2027, while conceding it may never match InnoLight or Eoptolink.

It seems like now it's a late 2027 into early 2028 event', because customers competing with NVIDIA concluded they need to deploy a lot more optics and to do so sooner. Hurlston called the near-term NPO opportunity larger than the CPO opportunity, with a higher adoption rate of optical lanes than NVIDIA's, and said NPO customers are requiring Lumentum to ship the entire ELS rather than bare laser chips. The consequence is capacity: NPO 'is going to put a lot of pressure on that Greensboro fab', Lumentum needs a 'next leg of the stool' and is trying to lock up NPO business now to fill Greensboro and more, but would require an NVIDIA-style commitment before funding further capacity. NVIDIA underwrote Greensboro with a long-term agreement characterised as a multibillion-dollar deal plus an investment that helped Lumentum buy, equip and outfit the fab, acquired early calendar 2026 and not operational until early calendar 2028; the team running it was inherited from Qorvo, and qualification at NVIDIA itself took a year.

The reverse risk is tit-for-tat curtailment of Chinese sub-component supply - substrates, isolators and other raw materials Lumentum currently relies on - against which its manufacturing footprint in Thailand, in China itself and in the United Kingdom (a safe harbour on substrates) is the hedge.

Wupen Yuen framed the same ladder as scale-across 1, scale-out 10, scale-up 100, scale-in 1,000, and positioned Lumentum as 'going all the way from scale across to scale out, to scale up, and later to scale in'.

quarterly_data.signal: Post-earnings supply update: the supply-demand gap is 'still extending' and Lumentum is 'still short everywhere' - DML short, CW laser short. Yuen does not see the shortage going away in 2027; the industry forecasts scale-out module volume doubling from 2026 to 2027 while laser supply does not catch up, and 2028 scale-up drives another 3 to 4x increase of demand, so the laser supply-demand gap does not close within the next couple of years. Lumentum is still allocating capacity, in some cases on pricing and expedite fees, to serve the most profitable opportunities, and 'all the deals we are making today are equal or higher pricing than the escalated pricing that we already had before' - management's own read that the gap persists.

quarterly_data.signal: Yuen reframed optical scale-up as an industry-wide story rather than the single-customer CPO story assumed at OFC: to serve 2028 optical scale-up volume the industry needs both CPO and NPO approaches, and by volume 'CPO will be half of the market. NPO is the other half of the market' - roughly 50/50. On the content Lumentum sells, CPO is 'an exclusive external light source market'; half of NPO also goes external light source (ELS) and the remaining roughly 25% of the overall market is still being debated between integrated light source (ILS) and ELS, with more and more movement toward ELS because the optical engine sits so close to the accelerator heat source that an integrated laser becomes the reliability-limiting factor. Even the ILS case will not use pluggable-class lasers: an NPO engine '1 inch by half an inch' packs 6.4T versus half an iPhone for a 1.6T module today, so fewer but higher-power lasers are required and the entire NPO/CPO application moves to '120, 150 milliwatt and above', not the traditional 70 milliwatt pluggable laser. Chinese CW laser supply chatter is aimed at that pluggable market, not this one.

quarterly_data.signal: ECOC 2026 product demonstration (official press release, not a call): Lumentum announced its plan to demonstrate an eight-wavelength dense wavelength division multiplexing (DWDM) laser module in an External Laser Small Form Factor Pluggable (ELSFP). The module's optical interface is designed to meet the applicable requirements of the Optical Compute Interconnect Multi-Source Agreement (OCI MSA), and it is intended for external laser source applications in co-packaged optics (CPO) and near-packaged optics (NPO) architectures. It provides eight simultaneous DWDM wavelengths across two four-channel bands centered near 1311 nm and 1331 nm; the design targets wavelength accuracy of +/-0.2 nm and demonstrates up to 24 dBm (~250 mW) of optical output power per wavelength at the fiber, with all eight channels operating simultaneously from a single pluggable module at approximately 12 W of power consumption. The module uses Lumentum's Ultra High Power (UHP) laser platform, already in production, in an eight-channel configuration. Lumentum expects initial availability of the DWDM ELSFP module with an OCI MSA optical interface in the first half of calendar year 2027. Sri Venkat (SVP and GM, Components) called CPO and NPO 'defining architectures for AI scale-up' and external laser sources 'a critical building block of that shift', and said the demonstration positions Lumentum to serve customers as the CPO/NPO market scales.
quarterly_data.figure: eight DWDM wavelengths in two four-channel bands near 1311 nm and 1331 nm; wavelength accuracy target +/-0.2 nm; up to 24 dBm (~250 mW) per wavelength at the fiber; approximately 12 W module power; initial availability expected in the first half of calendar year 2027

quarterly_data.signal: ECOC 2026 joint demonstration (official press release, not a call): Lumentum announced plans for a joint board-level demonstration with Qualcomm Technologies and Corning of a high-density die-to-die (D2D) optical interconnect for AI scale-up architectures, combining a D2D interface IP subsystem from Qualcomm Technologies with Lumentum's VCSEL-based optical interconnect platform and Corning multimode fiber connectivity. The massively parallel optical D2D architecture is designed for future co-packaged optics (CPO) and near-packaged optics (NPO) implementations supporting emerging D2D interfaces such as UCIe, extending high-density D2D connectivity over multimode-fiber optical links spanning tens of meters while maintaining low latency and power consumption. The proof-of-concept configuration uses optical channels operating at 32 Gb/s NRZ; the architecture is designed to support approximately 1 Tb/s/mm of shoreline bandwidth density today, with line of sight to approximately 4 Tb/s/mm through higher lane rates and increased channel density. This is a proof-of-concept demonstration; the release gives no product availability date, customer or commercial terms.
quarterly_data.figure: 32 Gb/s NRZ optical channels (proof-of-concept); approximately 1 Tb/s/mm shoreline bandwidth density today, line of sight to approximately 4 Tb/s/mm

quarterly_data.signal: The D2D demonstration's optical interconnect uses Lumentum's optical engine based on advanced-packaged 1060 nm VCSEL technology, with approximately 10 Tb/s of aggregate transmit and receive capacity and high-density two-dimensional VCSEL and photodetector arrays with backside lens technology. The platform is built on Lumentum's ultra-high-volume 3D sensing manufacturing base and is designed to support high shoreline bandwidth density, signal integrity and energy-efficient optical connectivity for board-level and system-level AI scale-up architectures. CTO Matt Sysak said the demonstration shows how Lumentum's 1060 nm VCSEL platform can bring high-density optical connectivity closer to AI compute, and described it as showing 'a practical path toward compact, energy-efficient optical D2D links for next-generation AI scale-up architectures'.

quarterly_data.signal: Six-inch indium phosphide ramp running ahead of plan: Coherent significantly increased InP production in Q2 and is on track to double internal InP production by the fourth quarter of calendar 2026. Current-quarter wafer starts are already at 80% of the doubling target, after wafer starts more than quadrupled from the September quarter to the December quarter; a wafer start takes about six months to become a transceiver shipment, so the benefit starts this quarter and builds over coming quarters. Production is ramping in parallel at Sherman, Texas and Yarfala, Sweden, with EMLs, CW lasers and photodiodes all in production on six-inch and six-inch yields exceeding three-inch yields. A six-inch wafer produces more than four times as many chips at less than half the cost; almost all capacity being added is six-inch, about half of capacity will be six-inch by the end of calendar 2026, and plans go well beyond doubling in following years. Coherent has multiple six-inch InP substrate suppliers and has secured committed substrate supply supporting the doubling; management called Coherent the world's only producer of six-inch indium phosphide.

quarterly_data.signal: PhotonLink formally launched at ECOC (pre-announced on the August earnings call). CMO Sanjai Parthasarathi introduced it as 'our integrated optics platform, purpose-built for AI data center connectivity', and CEO Jim Anderson set out its scope and rationale: it is a single integrated platform that is 'architecture agnostic, that works across CPO, NPO, chip-to-chip as well', and it exists because a number of customers 'came to us and asked' for 'the complete optical solution, the complete assembly' rather than components, since pulling together laser sources, fiber optic cable, complex optical assemblies and passive optics is the hard part of moving to optics. Anderson framed the transition it targets: telecom, scale-across and scale-out networks were long ago converted from electrical to optical, and over the coming years 'the only remaining electrical portions of the network' - the scale-up network and even chip-to-chip links - will become photonic. His end-to-end example for a switch or compute chip fed by an external laser source: Coherent supplies the complete ELS, the complete optical assembly from the ELS to the chip, and the complete optical assembly back out to the faceplate for photonic I/O. He argued only Coherent has the whole generate/shape/guide/detect technology set in-house, and cited 'hundreds of millions of components and optical assemblies' delivered as evidence it can ramp at data-center scale.
quarterly_data.figure: architecture agnostic across CPO, NPO and chip-to-chip; hundreds of millions of components and optical assemblies delivered

quarterly_data.signal: CEO Jim Anderson sized the opportunity PhotonLink opens: looking out to 2030, Coherent's addressable market for its existing portfolio products is 'about $60 billion', and PhotonLink 'allows us to access another $30 billion of integrated optics market opportunity by the end of this decade'. That integrated-optics figure is higher than the CPO/NPO addressable-market floor management gave on the August earnings call.
quarterly_data.figure: about $60 billion addressable market at 2030 for existing portfolio products; another $30 billion of integrated optics market opportunity by the end of this decade

quarterly_data.signal: CEO Jim Anderson put a dollar value on PhotonLink content: for a switch or processor chip that 'needs 100 terabit of I/O capacity' using '200 gig optical lanes', Coherent's content 'would be up to about $15,000 per system or per 100T chip' when Coherent brings all the content for the customer (the full PhotonLink solution).

He said there is 'not just a one size fits all' architecture - 'Some customers will adopt CPO right away. Some customers will first adopt NPO and then over time, move to CPO later on' - and that 'We have anchor customers already secured for both CPO as well as NPO architectures' (no customer named in his remarks).

New at the launch: NPO is expected 'to start to ramp in the second half of next calendar year' (calendar 2027), 'primarily for scale-up applications', and chip-to-chip optical links are 'a little further out', expected 'in the 2029, 2030 timeline', although customer design activity on chip-to-chip photonic connections is already intense.
quarterly_data.figure: CPO scale-out ramp in the December quarter (Q4 of this calendar year); CPO scale-up in the second half of 2027; NPO in the second half of next calendar year; chip-to-chip in the 2029, 2030 timeline

quarterly_data.signal: EVP of Semiconductor Devices Beck Mason said the 'generate' part of PhotonLink rests on four light-source platforms: ultra-high-power CW lasers, high-power CW lasers, VCSEL arrays and high-density VCSEL arrays. The ultra-high-power CW laser, where Coherent has 'really strong traction from a number of customers', sits remote from the transmission inside an external laser source (ELS) that 'contains up to eight ultra-high-power CW lasers'; each laser 'can typically feed multiple links, usually around four', supplying the photons for silicon photonic modulators co-packaged (CPO) or near-packaged (NPO) with the XPU or switch chip. It is designed for high output power (one laser split and shared across several links, lowering cost), high power-conversion efficiency (lower system power dissipation) and very low phase and amplitude noise (better bit error rate), and he said these lasers 'exceed all of our customer requirements'. On this platform Coherent has 'two long-term agreements signed with leading hyperscale AI data center customers for both CPO and NPO solutions'.
quarterly_data.figure: ELS holds up to eight ultra-high-power CW lasers, each usually feeding around four links; two long-term agreements with leading hyperscale AI data center customers for CPO and NPO

quarterly_data.signal: EVP Beck Mason said the second light source, a high-power buried heterostructure CW laser, serves NPO designs that embed the laser in the module, co-packaged with the silicon photonic modulator, instead of using a remote ELS. Its smaller size, lower power dissipation and high efficiency suit that role, he called it 'flexible and replaceable', and it is already a volume part: 'we are already shipping millions of units a month' because it is used widely in Coherent's pluggable data-center transceivers, with proven field reliability - 'It is production-ready now.' He added that Coherent has 'shipped over 300 million indium phosphide lasers to the field so far, and the pace of that is only ramping up'.
quarterly_data.figure: already shipping millions of units a month; over 300 million indium phosphide lasers shipped to the field so far

quarterly_data.signal: EVP Beck Mason said VCSEL arrays 'enable the lowest energy per bit for NPO applications' and very high channel counts in a dense package, giving 'the lowest cost and the best bandwidth density' of any option for integrated photonic links. He described two types for NPO: Type 1 conventional and Type 2 high density (the high-density 2D VCSEL he covered next as 'the other area', in production in the second half of calendar 2027). Type 1 is designed for ribbon fiber assemblies and is similar to what Coherent has sold for many years; Coherent has been 'supplying VCSEL arrays and PD arrays for more than 10 years' and he said it is 'the world's largest supplier of Datacom VCSELs today' (used in pluggable transceivers). In that Type 1 discussion he said the new arrays are 'high-density arrays. That means they are 2-dimensional', with more VCSEL channels, in flip-chip versions that mount directly on driver ICs; the photodiodes are likewise flip-chip for mounting on TIAs, and backside integrated lenses give more relaxed coupling, higher coupling efficiency and better link performance. 'These solutions will be production-ready in the first half of next calendar year.'
quarterly_data.figure: supplying VCSEL arrays and PD arrays for more than 10 years; says it is the world's largest supplier of Datacom VCSELs; new 2D flip-chip arrays (Type 1 discussion) production-ready in the first half of next calendar year

quarterly_data.signal: EVP Beck Mason previewed the high-density 2D VCSEL for NPO (the 'ultra-dense VCSEL arrays' of his summary), which Coherent was demonstrating in its booth on the ECOC floor: the VCSELs are so tightly spaced that the whole array couples into a single multi-core fiber. Coherent makes 'fibers with up to 37 separate cores' and has 'a VCSEL array and a PD array with 37 elements', flip-chipped with backside lenses - 'the most dense solution we have out there', giving very high capacity in a single fiber. It suits both PAM4 and NRZ ('slow and wide' as well as 'fairly fast and narrow'). 'These will be in production in the second half of calendar 2027.'
quarterly_data.figure: fibers with up to 37 separate cores; VCSEL and PD arrays with 37 elements; in production in the second half of calendar 2027

quarterly_data.signal: EVP Beck Mason said Coherent has 'shipped over 1 billion photodetectors to the field, both short-wave gallium arsenide and long-wave indium phosphide', and its 'latest generation of photodiodes goes all the way up to 200G today, and we have 400G devices in development'. The photodiodes can be flip-chipped directly onto TIAs with backside integrated lenses for better coupling efficiency, serving the receive end of the CPO link.
quarterly_data.figure: over 1 billion photodetectors shipped; photodiodes up to 200G today; 400G devices in development

quarterly_data.signal: EVP Beck Mason said all the devices Coherent makes come from its own wafer fabs - '4 major wafer fabs that are spread out across the globe': Sherman, Texas, 'arguably the world's largest and most advanced indium phosphide and gallium arsenide fab', running 6-inch InP and 6-inch GaAs lines; Jarfalla, Sweden, 6-inch InP, in production for over 2 decades and where some of the most advanced devices were developed; Zurich, Switzerland, historically the GaAs fab running 6-inch VCSELs in very high volume for Datacom and now also ramping 6-inch InP 'to enable the immense ramp we're seeing in demand on high-power lasers for PhotonLink and CPO applications'; and Fremont, California, running a 3-inch production line where many of the most advanced devices are developed. 'We're expanding capacity in all of these fabs today.'
quarterly_data.figure: 4 major wafer fabs: Sherman, Texas (6-inch InP and GaAs), Jarfalla, Sweden (6-inch InP), Zurich, Switzerland (6-inch VCSELs, now ramping 6-inch InP), Fremont, California (3-inch line); expanding capacity in all of them

quarterly_data.signal: EVP Beck Mason said laser capacity expansion 'has really been driven by our 6-inch transition', with gallium arsenide first: 'About 6 years ago, we transitioned all of our gallium arsenide production over to 6-inch' (run in Sherman, Texas and Zurich), the last piece - the pump laser platforms - moved to 6-inch around last year, and over that period GaAs line capacity rose 'by about a factor of 4'; Coherent now has 'capacity for over 1 billion VCSEL arrays per year'. Indium phosphide is following the same path - 'We're now transitioning all of our indium phosphide lines to 6-inch' - with the bulk of its high-power CW lasers, EMLs and photodiodes already qualified on 6-inch and ramping.
quarterly_data.figure: GaAs line capacity up by about a factor of 4 through the 6-inch transition; capacity for over 1 billion VCSEL arrays per year; all InP lines transitioning to 6-inch

quarterly_data.signal: CTO Julie Eng said isolators - which protect the laser from unwanted back reflection that otherwise harms the performance of the link - are becoming a key component in the CPO and NPO ramp, and that Coherent has customers securing capacity for garnet and isolators with long-term agreements. Coherent is vertically integrated in garnet, the magneto-optic material isolators are based on: it grows the garnet boule in the U.S., slices it into substrates and polishes them, grows garnet epitaxy on top, dices them and attaches polarizers, and she said it supplies 'a significant fraction of the industry's garnet and isolators today'.
quarterly_data.figure: no specific figure

quarterly_data.signal: CTO Julie Eng described the external laser source (ELS) as an integration platform: Coherent combines the laser with its own coupling lenses, isolator, ELS fiber assembly and thermoelectric cooler (which keeps the laser at a constant temperature), all internal components it designs and manufactures before integrating them into the ELS, which she said lets it respond faster to customer specifications. The lenses that focus the light into the isolator and fiber are glass molded lenses for efficient light coupling, in production by the end of this calendar year; Coherent has shipped a quarter billion lenses across its lens portfolio. ELS assembly and test is built on Coherent's transceiver line, and Coherent is sampling ELSs to customers today.
quarterly_data.figure: ELS sampling to customers today; glass molded lenses in production by the end of this calendar year; a quarter billion lenses shipped

quarterly_data.signal: CTO Julie Eng said Coherent has had internal fiber design and manufacturing for 25 years and has shipped over 300 million meters of fiber, but it focuses only on hard-to-make specialty fiber and does not compete in standard commodity SMF or MMF. Its polarization-maintaining fiber - key for silicon photonics in the remote-laser CPO architecture - is production-ready now, and its multi-core fiber serves the highly dense VCSEL-array solutions for NPO, CPO and chip-to-chip. She said Coherent is executing 'a very significant fiber manufacturing expansion for both CPO and NPO'.
quarterly_data.figure: 25 years of in-house fiber; over 300 million meters shipped; very significant fiber manufacturing expansion for CPO and NPO

quarterly_data.signal: CTO Julie Eng said Coherent is introducing two products at ECOC 2026: a Mode-Matched Fiber that improves coupling efficiency to edge-coupled silicon photonics, and a detachable FAU (fiber attach unit) connector that helps with serviceability and installation.
quarterly_data.figure: no specific figure

quarterly_data.signal: CTO Julie Eng walked through the parts Coherent makes to couple light from the fiber into silicon photonics: microlens arrays lithographically formed in silicon (precisely uniform from one lens to the next), Prism Micro Lens Arrays that also turn the light for grating-coupled silicon photonics, and precisely V-groove-etched fiber guides that hold the fiber. It integrates these with its polarization-maintaining fiber into a fiber attach unit (FAU), and can integrate all the FAUs into a precision fiber assembly that routes and protects the fibers for ease of deployment and less fiber damage. She said all of these are either in production now, by the end of this year or early next year.
quarterly_data.figure: either in production now, by the end of this year or early next year

quarterly_data.signal: CTO Julie Eng said that once fiber inside the rack reaches very high amounts, reducing fiber count becomes very important to customers, and Coherent makes three in-production parts for it: circulators, which combine signals going in opposite directions onto the same fiber and reduce fiber count by a factor of 2 (built on garnet plus yttrium vanadate crystal, which Coherent also designs and manufactures internally); WDM multiplexers that combine many wavelengths, relying on super-precision optical coatings Coherent delivers at scale; and fiber shuffles that organize high-density fiber routing and help reduce fiber breakage. Circulators and WDM multiplexers can be placed in the fiber shuffle, in the ELS or in connectors.
quarterly_data.figure: circulators reduce fiber count by a factor of 2; all in production

quarterly_data.signal: CTO Julie Eng said Coherent has an in-house silicon photonics design team, uses multiple foundries (as is common in the silicon industry) and does assembly and test in-house; it has demonstrated 200G-per-lane silicon photonics and is shipping it in production in its transceivers today. At OFC in March of this year it demonstrated a 400 gigabit link based on silicon photonics, on the show floor and in a post-deadline paper, and she said Coherent is, to her knowledge, the only one in the world to have shown that.
quarterly_data.figure: 200G per lane silicon photonics in production; 400 gigabit silicon photonics link demonstrated at OFC

quarterly_data.signal: CTO Julie Eng detailed Coherent's 6.4T Silicon Photonics NPO module, shown at OFC and again at ECOC: it integrates silicon photonics modulators and photodetectors with drivers, TIAs and all the optical coupling in 32 lanes of 200G, and as a socketed NPO it delivers 15 gigabits per second per millimeter. It can be fed by a remote ELS through Coherent's FAU and precision fiber assembly or have the laser integrated into the silicon photonics NPO, and the same 6.4T silicon photonics provides the modulation and detection in Coherent's end-to-end CPO solution.
quarterly_data.figure: 6.4T; 32 lanes of 200G; 15 gigabits per second per millimeter

quarterly_data.signal: CTO Julie Eng presented Coherent's VCSEL-based NPOs. The VCSEL NPO shown at OFC integrates the VCSEL, photodiodes, drivers, TIAs and coupling optics into a single deployable NPO. The NPO built on the 2D VCSEL array integrates the substrates, drivers and TIAs, 2D VCSELs, 2D photodiode arrays, a heat spreader and a lens array, and has been demonstrated at 1.2 picojoules per bit, which she said is, as far as she knows, the lowest CPO or NPO power consumption including the laser. A second NPO built on the high-density VCSEL and photodiode, integrated with TIAs and drivers, can take the light out the top or out the side (adding a turning mirror, lenses and a lensed fiber array).
quarterly_data.figure: 1.2 picojoules per bit, including the laser

quarterly_data.signal: CTO Julie Eng laid out the CPO vs NPO trade-off: CPO puts the optical engine literally on the package of the switch or XPU chip and offers the lowest power consumption and, in many cases, the highest density, while NPO moves the optics off the package onto the board right next to it - easier to deploy and more serviceable, but moving it away from the chip costs power and the socket impacts signal integrity. NPO is also an architectural platform: a common form factor and socket can accommodate either silicon photonics or VCSELs, and Coherent is a founder of the Open CPX MSA, helping develop an open ecosystem for a common connector among vendors to give customers architectural flexibility.
quarterly_data.figure: no specific figure

quarterly_data.signal: CTO Julie Eng said interest in chip-to-chip optical interconnect has grown a lot in the last 3-9 months (this calendar year): as bandwidth between compute and memory scales, the optical link moves from the edge of the package to the interior of the package - after the intercontinental, terrestrial, data-center and now in-rack shifts from electronics to photonics, 'the next frontier, inside the chip package'. Customers are looking at multiple architectures, including an ELS with ultra-high-power lasers, integrated lasers and high-density VCSEL solutions, and with so many lanes there is a lot of discussion of WDM, making circulators and WDM multiplexers 'a very important architectural tool'.
quarterly_data.figure: interest up over the last 3-9 months

quarterly_data.signal: CTO Julie Eng said Coherent has shipped over 650 million of the optical components she introduced for the PhotonLink shape, guide and receive stages and is in high volume in all of them. She pitched the breadth of the portfolio as making Coherent a 'trusted advisor': because it has all the technologies, it can give a customer an honest assessment of each architecture (with VCSELs, the power consumption and cost; with an integrated laser, the complexity and the impact on signal integrity) instead of selling one solution, and she said Coherent is 'definitely scaling all of these technologies and products today'.
quarterly_data.figure: over 650 million optical components shipped

quarterly_data.signal: In its ECOC 2026 release Coherent listed a technology demonstration (not a shipping product) of a compact 3.2T 2xDR4 pluggable transceiver architecture in an OSFP-size package, with dual 1.6T optical paths. The demonstration incorporates eight 425G PAM4 line-side optical lanes, Coherent Differential EMLs and Coherent photodiodes, which the company said highlights progress toward next-generation 400G-per-lane optical connectivity.

quarterly_data.signal: For DCI and scale-across, Coherent said it would showcase at ECOC 2026 its LS200 full C-band pluggable optical line system for datacenter interconnect and transport, a compact architecture that brings pluggable line-system functionality closer to the router or switch while supporting flexible point-to-point optical transport. Among new products and emerging technologies it also listed a Pluggable Optical Line System (POLS): a full C-band optical line system with a high-power, variable-gain amplifier in a compact QSFP form factor, designed for 800G ZR/ZR+ digital coherent optics, supporting up to 32 DWDM wavelengths over a single fiber pair and carrying up to 25.6Tbps across links from 2km to 200km.

quarterly_data.signal: Among the new products and emerging technologies across its optical networking portfolio that Coherent said it would showcase at ECOC 2026: FlexConnect, a detachable fiber array unit connector for CPO applications designed to simplify assembly and maintenance, with repeatable plug-unplug performance, interchangeability and an epoxy-free optical path compatible with high-power lasers; OptiAlign, a high-precision fiber array unit for CPO applications designed to support precise pitch control and high fiber-channel counts, combining an internally developed V-groove with customized fiber dimensions; OptiFocus, a two-in-one coupling lens design for ELS intended to simplify optical assembly while providing high coupling efficiency; FiberPack, a passive fiber assembly kit for scale-up and scale-out architectures integrating fiber attach, micro-lens, tray and termination technologies; and OptiPolar Array X, a multi-channel polarization beam splitter array in a super-compact form factor based on glass material, optimized for multi-lane systems.

Management frames InP as the crucial enabler of the ultra-fast optical and wireless data communications that data centers rely on, with IQE positioned by decades of InP epitaxy experience, and says hyperscale AI and data centers are "a massive opportunity for us across our materials portfolio, but especially in relation to indium phosphide."

That kind of conversion would again need to be tied to discrete customer demand and visibility to that, because obviously it does come with downtime of the tools and also CapEx commitments." On Taiwan 6-inch InP epitaxy: "We are monitoring demand very closely, and as mentioned, we are converting capacities if and when that demand materializes." Additional MOCVD tools would come via LTA, customer co-funding, or tool consignment - "any kind of capacity expansion or addition of tools will need to come with customer commitments." quarterly_data.signal: Balance sheet transformed after year end. The GBP 81 million fundraise - GBP 45 million from MACOM (GBP 30 million cash plus GBP 15 million of convertible loan notes), with the remainder from existing shareholders - closed the morning of this results call. Proceeds fully repay the HSBC revolving credit facility and redeem existing loan notes, "leaving us without bank debt," with net cash inflow to IQE of around GBP 27.9 million. Management does "not foresee any additional fundraisers in the future" absent a large customer-backed capacity expansion. The 18-month strategic review - which assessed options from a sale of Taiwan up to a full sale of the company - concluded that staying independent creates the best shareholder value.

Pluggables contribute the vast majority of silicon photonics revenue today. High-volume manufacturing of 200-gig-per-lane technology is underway, 400-gig capability has already been demonstrated, and the multiyear roadmap advances module enablement to 1.6T, 3.2T and beyond. GF has more than 40 silicon photonics customers, and CEO Tim Breen said GF is on track and potentially ahead of the growth targets set for end-2028 through 2030. quarterly_data.signal: SCALE, described as the industry's first OCI MSA compatible solution for near and co-packaged optics, has 7 ACTIVE ENGAGEMENTS with leading companies. GF taped out a SCALE-related design win in Q2 and expects to tape out another in Q3. Management reiterated a consistent timeline: the NPO ramp BEGINS IN 2027 and the CPO ramp BEGINS IN 2028. Because near and co-packaged optics are built on a common photonic IC - an EIC bonded to a PIC with a micro-optic and a fiber-attached unit - and differ mainly in that NPO is bonded to the board while CPO sits within the package (plus SerDes architecture differences), GF expects to benefit regardless of which form factor customers adopt. Many customers are pursuing both, with NPO ramping sooner. Breen attributed the sudden industry interest in NPO to SerDes synergies that make the system transition smaller than a jump straight to full CPO, and expects pluggables, NPO and CPO all to coexist in the data center.
quarterly_data.figure: 7 active SCALE engagements; 1 SCALE tape-out in Q2 and another expected in Q3; NPO ramp begins 2027, CPO ramp begins 2028

quarterly_data.signal: GF entered a letter of intent with the U.S. Department of Commerce for a $300 MILLION award to accelerate next-generation silicon photonics technologies in the U.S. The funding supports three components: continued PIC-level innovation and improved modulator technology to reach 400-gig per lane and beyond; NEW MATERIALS to be introduced into the system - management named barium titanate, thin-film lithium niobate and indium phosphide; and packaging capability and capacity for the integrated optical engines needed for near and co-packaged optics, building directly on the SCALE platform. Management said the endorsement came from the world's top XPU providers, hyperscalers, AI connectivity leaders and ecosystem partners.
quarterly_data.figure: $300M U.S. Department of Commerce letter of intent for next-generation silicon photonics

quarterly_data.signal: Silicon germanium is OVERSUBSCRIBED THROUGHOUT 2027 and, notably, GF's SiGe business is LARGER THAN ITS SILICON PHOTONICS BUSINESS TODAY. GF secured multiple new SiGe TIA and driver design wins across networking customers in the quarter. The growth has two compounding drivers: the shift to optical networking itself, and the fact that what could previously be done in CMOS at 50-gig and 100-gig per lane cannot be done at 200-gig and definitely not at 400-gig per lane, forcing transimpedance amplifiers and increasingly the drivers out into high-performance analog processes like SiGe. High-performance analog also appears in near and co-packaged optics depending on architecture. GF is expanding SiGe capacity at Burlington, Vermont and qualifying 300-millimeter SiGe in Singapore for additional capacity, better economics and higher fT/fMAX performance. The SiGe lineage traces to IBM Microelectronics, which invented SiGe and is part of GF today.
quarterly_data.figure: SiGe oversubscribed throughout 2027; SiGe business larger than silicon photonics today; Vermont capacity expanding, 300mm SiGe qualifying in Singapore

quarterly_data.signal: Capacity strategy is a structural advantage: GF is adding capacity WITHIN ITS EXISTING FAB FOOTPRINT rather than building new fabs, which management contrasted with competitors on longer lead times. Breen said GF 'could 10x our photonics capacity within our current 4 walls' globally on its long-term plan. Q2 utilization was in the high 80s, leaving about 10 points of headroom to grow into with installed capacity. Confidence in bringing capacity online plus factory productivity improvements was cited as a direct contributor to raising the full-year CID outlook. On competition in silicon photonics, Breen said customers are coming to GF saying they do not have enough capacity secured and want more, partly to mitigate geopolitical risk, and he sees no customer-concentration concern given 40-plus customers.
quarterly_data.figure: Photonics capacity expandable ~10x within existing fabs; Q2 utilization high-80s with ~10 points of headroom

quarterly_data.signal: GF implemented PRICING INCREASES in partnership with customers across several technology corridors during Q2, following what management called constructive conversations. The adjustments will be reflected in revenue COMMENCING IN 2027, with magnitude varying by end market and technology based on differentiated value, supply/demand dynamics and inflationary absorption. GF will continue assessing 2027 pricing through the second half of 2026.

quarterly_data.signal: GF launched Quantum Technology Solutions in May 2026, a dedicated team aimed at taking the quantum industry from prototypes to high-volume production. The strategy is qubit-agnostic across superconducting, trapped ion, photonic, topological and spin modalities, using the FDX platform as a cryogenic CMOS foundation and extending advanced packaging into the cryogenic regime for 3D heterogeneous integration. GF is working with 8 of the world's leading quantum computing players including PsiQuantum, Quantinuum and Quantum Motion plus endorsements from the quantum arms of large hyperscalers, and has already begun 4 new customer-specific engagements in the three months since launch. The effort is anchored by an expected $375 MILLION grant from the U.S. Department of Commerce. Over the next 1 to 3 years quantum revenue comes largely through engineering engagements booked in technology services, with manufacturing-services revenue ramping toward the end of the decade. Several quantum players are working on the photonics side of their solutions, which maps directly onto GF's silicon photonics roadmap.
quarterly_data.figure: $375M expected U.S. Department of Commerce quantum grant; 8 leading quantum players engaged; 4 new customer engagements in 3 months

quarterly_data.signal: IP, software and custom silicon: GF completed the acquisition of the Synopsys ARC processor IP Solutions business in June, adding CPU, DSP, NPU and RISC-V technologies, a software development toolkit and application-specific processor design capability - over 150 patents, 300 existing customers and 400 R&D engineers. Combined with MIPS, this lets GF engage customers earlier in the design cycle for edge AI and on-device inference in automotive, industrial and robotics. Full-year 2026 technology services contribution from MIPS plus ARC was RAISED to $100-120 million from a prior $60-100 million, skewed roughly one third Q3 and two thirds Q4, and technology services revenue is now expected toward the high end of the 10-12% of total revenue range with gross margin significantly above corporate targets. Design wins in the quarter included 3 strategic chiplet wins with Lockheed Martin on FinFET and FDX, an expanded FinFET win with Microchip, a first-ever PMIC design win with MediaTek on the BCD platform, an ADAS radar tape-out for Bosch on FDX, and a new microLED display backplane win for augmented reality wearables at a leading hyperscaler.
quarterly_data.figure: Technology services contribution raised to $100M-$120M for 2026 (from $60M-$100M); ARC adds 150 patents, 300 customers, 400 R&D engineers

quarterly_data.signal: CEO Tim Breen on the silicon photonics growth targets: 'the industry adoption needed to reach those targets has already happened. So I think we now have very limited adoption risk baked into that.' The constraint is now supply, not demand - 'All indicators right now from a demand point of view are flashing kind of bright green relative to those targets... we see much more demand than we can supply out of our current install base, so we will definitely be accelerating that.' Pluggables alone get GF 'pretty much all the way' to the first milestone, with NPO rollout already picking up steam on top. The upside case is co-packaged optics: if CPO sees really broad adoption in the latter part of the period GF 'could blow past those targets materially', because CPO is the technology for the scale-up transition and 'you are replacing 10x the links of scale-out with those solutions, so you are not going to see a linear growth story'.
quarterly_data.figure: co-packaged optics replaces 10x the links of scale-out

quarterly_data.signal: First photonics customer count disclosed: 'We have more than 40 customers in photonics today, and that number keeps growing as players really invest in their optical roadmap.' Breen added that 'everyone who was touting copper two years ago has either launched an organic or inorganic effort to get into optical'. On the form-factor transition, near-package optics and co-packaged optic designs are 'even taping out in our fabs today' and are 'going into production in 2027 and 2028', while pluggable optical transceivers ramp strongly now; the NPO rollout is being led by 'many of the same players who are in pluggables today'. The core photonics platform roadmap runs from 100 gig per lane to 200 gig per lane to 400 gig per lane and beyond with new materials and modulators, paired with advanced packaging (hybrid bonding, fiber-to-chip attach) as the optical link moves closer to the XPU and switch ASIC.
quarterly_data.figure: more than 40 customers in photonics; NPO and CPO designs taping out today and going into production in 2027 and 2028; 100 gig per lane to 200 to 400 gig per lane roadmap

quarterly_data.signal: Breen put GF squarely in a supply-constrained posture for the next couple of years: 'We are clearly in a chasing supply moment today'; 'for the next couple of years, we will be more in a supply-constrained than a demand-constrained environment'. Job number one is ramping technologies GF already produces to higher volumes, and capex is going up again - 'We already are increasing our CapEx this year from last year. We'll be increasing further again next year' - with tool install and qualification speed, not demand, the thing that 'will gate or accelerate our growth going into next year'. Two new-cycle features: customers are co-investing financially alongside GF in the ramps ('customer skin in the game... they are willing to put capital to work'), and government partnerships provide tools that let GF 'accelerate CapEx at significant recovery rates that were not there in the past'.
quarterly_data.figure: capex increasing this year versus last year and increasing further again next year; supply-constrained, not demand-constrained, for the next couple of years

quarterly_data.signal: Progress against the long-term model GF 'laid out early this year': GF set targets for communication infrastructure and data center of '30% or in the 30s' and, per Breen, 'We are doing 60 in Q2' - well ahead of plan in that segment. Automotive is tracking in line with the long-term plan and IoT slightly ahead year to date. Breen said he does 'not see a demand constraint to meeting and exceeding that plan' and that the diversification across platforms 'may even make those numbers look a bit conservative'.

quarterly_data.signal: Mobile mix and a new read-across on foundry tightness: GF was 'more than 50% mobile going back a couple of years', is 'down to the mid-30s today' and the long-term model takes it to 'the mid-20s', with absolute mobile revenue assumed relatively flat rather than growing. 2026 is a tough year in mobile but 'not as tough at the higher end', where GF has more of its exposure. The new behaviour is that handset customers are now booking forward supply: 'mobile companies were the first to the queue in COVID... Now they are worried about being late when the data center is the one pushing all the demand. You are seeing actually more visibility where they are actually still saying, I need my supply for 2027. I need my supply for 2028.'
quarterly_data.figure: mobile more than 50% of revenue a couple of years ago, mid-30s today, mid-20s in the long-term model; handset customers booking supply for 2027 and 2028

quarterly_data.signal: Quantum status update since the Q2 call: 'today we announced that we completed the deal that we announced earlier in the year with the government', a partnership that accelerates GF's investment in infrastructure, tooling and PDK enablement for the more exotic processes - compressing a plan Breen framed as 'What would it take to do those in 2 years instead of over 5, 6 years?'. He stressed the roadmap is not orthogonal to the rest of GF: the exotic materials being proven for quantum - thin-film lithium niobate and barium titanate - 'will be needed for the next generation of photonics', i.e. the next generation of photonic modulators. The platform rests on cryo-CMOS (conventional FDSOI CMOS characterised at 4 degrees Kelvin) for qubit readout, plus novel-material integration, advanced packaging and high-speed photonic interconnect.
quarterly_data.figure: government partnership compressing a 5, 6 year plan into 2 years; cryo-CMOS characterised at 4 degrees Kelvin

quarterly_data.signal: GF delivered on its objective to roughly double silicon photonics revenue within the CID end market, to over $200 million in 2025. Even on this higher base it expects to NEARLY DOUBLE the silicon photonics contribution again in 2026, driven by strong customer demand, a robust ramp in supply capacity and the integration of Advanced Micro Foundry (AMF, Singapore), whose acquisition closed in November last year and is expected to be accretive to corporate gross margin targets in 2026. As pluggable applications ramp and co-packaged optics begins to scale, management now believes GF is on a path to a $1 billion run rate revenue level for silicon photonics by the end of 2028 - 'a substantial acceleration from our prior objective.' The majority of photonics revenue today is in the pluggable space, and silicon photonics comes through at a highly accretive gross margin.
quarterly_data.figure: silicon photonics revenue over $200 million in 2025; nearly double in 2026; $1 billion run rate revenue level by the end of 2028

quarterly_data.signal: In Q4 GF secured an important co-packaged optics design win for scale-up networks on its CLO silicon photonics platform, with photonic IC design wins at both endpoints of the scale-up network - 'an important step in the industry's rollout of CPO.' Breen said the CPO transition was always 'a '27 scale ramp more than a '26 scale ramp', and design wins and tape-out planning indicate it is on track because 'CPO is the only way to address certain performance workloads, especially on scale up networks'; the form-factor changes will drive significant increases of content. Technology roadmap: an offering for 200 gig per lane technologies today and a road map to 400 gig per lane and beyond; the InfiniLink design team in Cairo, Egypt helps customers building co-packaged optics solutions onboard faster; the collaboration with Corning brings detachable fiber attach, which management called critical for the transition to co-packaged optics; silicon photonics is being scaled in Singapore and the U.S., including on a 300-millimeter platform.
quarterly_data.figure: CPO design win for scale-up networks in Q4; CPO a '27 scale ramp; 200 gig per lane today, road map to 400 gig per lane

quarterly_data.signal: Capacity and capex: FY2026 non-IFRS net capex is expected at 15% to 20% of full year revenue (versus 2025 net capex of approximately $574 million, or 8% of revenue), driven primarily by strong customer demand in capacity corridors where GF is OVERSUBSCRIBED - silicon photonics, FDX and SiGe - plus establishing new capabilities such as advanced packaging. Breen: 'those corridors are running hot'; GF is meeting customer demand today, but the ramp profiles of designs already won and now taping out require investment, done within the existing 4-wall footprint (New York, Burlington and a legacy facility being converted in Germany) with quick ramps, good capital efficiency and eligibility for government support. High-performance SiGe (TIAs and driver ICs) is pulled through by pluggable optical transceivers, and that capacity is being 'very, very well utilized' today. 2025 gross capex was up about 15% but net capex down about 7% as government support in the U.S., Germany and Singapore began to flow, expected to grow again in 2026. 2026 free cash flow margin is guided to approximately 10% of revenue as GF receives customer prepayments. Footprint: a $16 billion U.S. investment commitment (June 2025) to expand manufacturing and advanced packaging in New York and Vermont, and a EUR 1.1 billion Dresden expansion to over 1 million wafers per year by the end of 2028.

quarterly_data.signal: Design-win momentum and acquisitions: a record over 500 design wins in 2025, over 95% on a sole-source basis, with active engagements across all 4 U.S. hyperscalers, all 5 top automotive OEMs, all 6 mobile fabless and OEM and 7 of the top 8 industrial IDMs. New design wins driven specifically by GF's manufacturing footprint were worth well over $3 billion of combined expected lifetime revenue in 2025. contracts.signal: CEO Bill Brennan named xAI as the customer that created the ZeroFlap concept: while building in another data center xAI was 'struggling mightily with link flaps' and could not keep cluster availability above even 90%. Moving into its own liquid-cooled data center, 'they came to us and said... What we want you to do is extend your AEC family from 3 meters to 7 meters because if you can do 7 meters, we can cover every connection in the row, and we can build a ZeroFlap cluster.' Brennan notes this is the ONLY transition where copper has replaced optical, for lengths up to 7 meters. He visited Memphis over the summer: xAI has achieved 99.9% uptime and can bring a cluster up in 5 days versus 6 to 8 weeks.
contracts.units: AEC family extended from 3 meters to 7 meters

connects_to.relationship: ZeroFlap Optics with real-time link telemetry for NIC-to-first-switch connections longer than 7 meters

contracts.signal: Oracle named as the customer behind the telemetry version of ZeroFlap: 'After we made this transition, Oracle came to us and said, Look, we'd love to address these problems as well, but our connections between the NIC and the first switch are longer than 7 meters, and we can't redesign. We've got what we've got.' Credo designed a custom DSP plus a software platform that lights up continuous real-time telemetry on each of the six links between a GPU and a switch (three in each direction), measuring eye height, SNR, post-FEC bit error rates and histograms to create a yellow 'check engine light' for a link instead of only green or red; it also identifies multipath interference caused by dust on the fiber plant and latent ESD damage, and mitigates likely link flaps by taking a link down in an orderly way rather than disrupting the cluster.

quarterly_data.signal: AECs grew again, driven by existing customers and new wins INCLUDING A FIFTH HYPERSCALER, with demand accelerating at hyperscalers and emerging Neocloud providers. Brennan: AECs are now the de facto standard for intra-rack and rack-to-rack connectivity up to 7 meters, increasingly displacing laser-based optical modules; ZeroFlap AECs deliver up to 1,000x better reliability than commodity laser-based optics at roughly half the power. Large-scale deployments run at 100 gig per lane with a long tail; 1.6-terabit AECs will support Ethernet, UALink and ESUN, and PCIe Gen6 AECs are sampling now for mass production in first half fiscal '27. At 200 gig per lane the value proposition is stronger with an ASP uplift, though reach shrinks 'from 7 meters to 5 meters'. Credo's strength is scale-out (with front end coming along; a couple of customers deploying in switch racks / disaggregated chassis); front end is expected to be 20% to 25% of the scale-out market. Brennan on 200G: 'NVIDIA is going to lead the charge with Vera Rubin, but many other customers will follow on a slower time line', and that market will be addressed by AECs plus laser-based modules, with ALCs ramping in.
quarterly_data.figure: fifth hyperscaler; up to 1,000x better reliability at roughly half the power; up to 7 meters (from 7 meters to 5 meters at 200G); PCIe Gen6 AECs mass production first half fiscal '27

quarterly_data.signal: ZeroFlap Optics PULLED IN: progress is ahead of schedule - production shipments began with the first Neocloud customer, Tensor Wave (joint announcement covering both AECs and ZF Optics), and 3 additional customers including hyperscalers and Neocloud operators are in qualification. Last quarter Credo signaled a second-half fiscal '27 ramp; it now expects a significant production ramp beginning in the first quarter of fiscal '27 and continuing through the year - 'we pulled in 6 months', driven by customer pull. Brennan: 'We've got 4 in now' and expects more than 4 customers ramping during fiscal '27. ZF Optics adds continuous link-flap telemetry and autonomous mitigation via the Pilot software with switch-level SDK integration - the first time an optical transceiver has been taken up the stack to deliver real-time telemetry - and lets Credo address optical connectivity at any length inside the data center.
quarterly_data.figure: ramp pulled in 6 months to the first quarter of fiscal '27; 4 in now, more than 4 expected; 3 additional customers in qualification

quarterly_data.signal: IC business (optical DSPs and retimers across 50G/100G/200G per lane): strong optical DSP growth expected in fiscal '26 on 100 gig per lane deployments, with increasing 200 gig traction as customers prepare for 1.6T transitions and 'a lot of uplift right now for LRO' as power becomes more important at 200 gig. Ethernet retimers growing significantly at 100 gig per lane in switching fabrics and AI servers; PCIe Gen6 retimer design wins in fiscal '26 expected to convert to production revenue in fiscal '27. Blue Heron, a 200 gig per lane retimer for scale-up supporting UALink, ESUN and Ethernet, announced its first customer, upscale AI, and Credo will build AECs with it. Brennan: 'We don't have any revenue for scale up' today - the bulk of AI revenue is scale-out. There will be an ASP uplift from 800 gig to 1.6T across the entire portfolio.

quarterly_data.signal: Three new multibillion-dollar TAM expansions: (1) Active LED cables (ALCs), built on micro LED expertise from the Hyperloom acquisition, bring AEC-class reliability, power and cost to mid-reach optical with a thinner gauge cable - reach initially up to 10 meters, then up to 30 meters; sample and qualify in fiscal '27, production ramp in fiscal '28. (2) OmniConnect gearboxes pair Credo's VSR SerDes with gearboxes for XPU connectivity: the first product, Weaver, enables up to a 10x improvement in memory beachfront I/O density at reach up to 10 inches by converting VSR to DDR; first customer Pozitron plans an inference XPU with 2 terabytes of memory capacity; first gearbox production ramp in fiscal '28, with future gearboxes for LPDDR6, PCIe Gen7/Gen6 scale-up and 200G/400G per lane making XPUs composable. (3) ZeroFlap Optics. Brennan positions Weaver as relief for the memory crunch by enabling DDR over HBM, 'probably the tightest area within the memory market right now'.
