quarterly_data.signal: CPO / ELSFP EXTERNAL LASER SOURCE ECONOMICS: ELSFP (external light source for co-packaged optics) is in very limited production now, ramping later in 2026 and through 2027 to ~400,000 PIECES PER MONTH IN 2028. Laser power scaling is the constraint: CPO/ELSFP uses a 300mW laser vs 70mW in an 800G transceiver and 100mW in a 1.6T transceiver, with die size ~6x larger, so meeting CPO demand requires the industry laser market to be 8-10x BIGGER than today; the next generation of ELSFP moves to DWDM, where yield loss is 40-50% worse than 1310nm. Laser capacity carries a 21-24 MONTH equipment-to-high-volume lead time. AOI is engaged with ~5 CPO customers on 3-4 year demand; several have already qualified AOI on fixed-wavelength CPO laser / ELSFP, with DWDM the current focus. High-volume ELSFP manufacturing is 'more like late Q3 next year' (late 2027). Houston laser fab capacity to grow ~300% by Q3 2027 plus a SECOND FAB cleanroom ~4x the size of the current facility (adding MOCVD, epi, steppers). Margin mix: laser gross margin 55-65%, ELSFP module ('EOSAP') >50%, both landing H2 2027. AOI is absent from first-generation CPO deployments purely because laser capacity must first feed AOI's own transceivers.
quarterly_data.figure: ELSFP ~400k pcs/month in 2028; 300mW CPO laser vs 70mW(800G)/100mW(1.6T); industry laser capacity needs 8-10x; laser GM 55-65%

quarterly_data.signal: BOTTLENECK HAS MOVED FROM LASERS TO DSP/TIA: because AOI makes its own lasers in-house it avoids the laser shortage that management calls 'the biggest bottleneck right now for the transceiver business' and 'the number one issue' for competitors; AOI's binding constraints for 800G/1.6T are instead DSP and TIA supply, where 'the whole supply chain is very tight' for 1.6T - AOI says its supplier ranks it FOURTH priority under a long-term partnership, with calls once or twice a week. INDIUM PHOSPHIDE SUBSTRATE: supply secured into end-2027 and 'incrementally better' than last quarter - not currently a limiter; AOI has just moved to 4-INCH substrate volume manufacturing and buys from 2 European + 2 Japanese + 3 Chinese suppliers, and is negotiating partnerships or a possible JOINT VENTURE with 2-3 of them for 2028-2029 volumes (laser capacity growing 'much more than a factor of 10'). Proprietary in-house production machinery insulates AOI from the industry's equipment-delivery bottlenecks.

Management expects sequential quarterly gross margin improvement of 25 to 50 basis points through the rest of fiscal 2026 (volume increases and new product introductions, net of cost increases such as gold and other precious metals). Full-year color (MACOM does not give full-year guidance): after 32% company growth last year, Telecom (which grew over 40% last year) is 'more likely going to be high single-digit, maybe low double-digit' - later 'thinking below 10% is a good way to think about it today' - and Industrial and Defense (close to 20% last year) is probably somewhere between 15-20%; internal targets put the company 'somewhere in the 20% range, plus or minus'. quarterly_data.signal: MACOM raised its fiscal 2026 Data Center year-over-year revenue growth base case from 20% to 35 to 40%, with upside that is 'a bit unquantifiable right now'. CEO Stephen Daly said 'the key underlying driver is 1.6T', where MACOM sees the most design wins transitioning into production runs; the Data Center backlog is very healthy and the second half should be stronger than the first half in absolute revenue dollars. Growth is primarily in pluggable optical modules and optical cables using its 800G and 1.6T PAM4 products (supporting DSP, LPO and LRO module architectures, plus coherent DCI including ZR and ZR Lite), and hyperscaler capital investments are robust. A significant portion of Data Center revenue is 400 gig and above with 1.6T the fastest-growing portion; 'The real action is at 200 gig per lane PAM4' and next-generation coherent, while 25 gig per lane NRZ is holding up, 50 gig per lane PAM4 is flat and 100 gig per lane PAM4 is solid. MACOM supports all of the US hyperscalers as well as international hyperscalers, selling to builders of modules, AOCs and cables. Management does not frame the growth as share gain: 'I think the market's growing. We're winning designs.' The product roadmap extends to 3.2T.
quarterly_data.figure: Data Center FY2026 growth base case raised from 20% to 35 to 40%

quarterly_data.signal: LPO, LRO and copper: MACOM now has three hyperscalers embracing LPO and is 'in various phases of production' with them - in all cases 100 gig per lane for generally 800 gig modules; management expects LPO to remain a small part of the market for the next one to two years and to evolve into NPO/CPO/XPO. Customers are also investigating LRO at 1.6T using 200 gig per lane chips, and management sees LRO as more likely to happen first than 1.6T LPO. LPO interest is also appearing in PCIe, NPO and telecom front haul. On copper, there is renewed interest in MACOM's linear equalizers to extend active copper cable (ACC) reach at 800G and 1.6T and for backplanes (eliminating retimers, and important at 400 gig per lane), but Q1 contained no ACC revenue; management sees the ACC opportunity as bigger than backplane equalizers, and some customers are evaluating converting AECs to ACCs. MACOM launched a PCIe 6 optical chipset supporting sideband data streams over fiber and a new PCIe 7 equalizer, giving it new exposure to the compute side of the data center network.
quarterly_data.figure: three hyperscalers in LPO production phases (100 gig per lane, 800 gig modules); no ACC revenue in Q1

quarterly_data.signal: Photonics and CPO/NPO: demand for MACOM's 200 gig per lane photodetectors (for 800G and 1.6T) continues to grow, with indications that demand will remain strong into calendar 2027; the indium phosphide photodetector business is growing rapidly, higher-speed photodetectors are in development, and EML lasers are in test. CW lasers: two customers - module makers, the first line of entry before a hyperscaler PCN process adds MACOM to the approved vendor list - have confirmed MACOM's 75-milliwatt CW lasers meet their requirements electrically for their silicon photonics solutions, followed by a qualification phase lasting 'some number of months' and a fab production-readiness review. CEO Stephen Daly called it 'a watershed moment because six months ago, we were not in a position where we had a compliant laser'; MACOM does not make 400-milliwatt class lasers and does not sell lasers into 1.6 applications today, so this would be share gain. The product set sold into CPO or NPO platforms is very similar to pluggables (drivers, TIAs, photodetectors and possibly lasers); these platforms are moving quickly to silicon photonics, putting heavy demand on CW laser and photodetector chips, with far more channels per chip, and some systems are moving to coherent light. MACOM's future products are increasingly optimized for CPO and NPO.
quarterly_data.figure: 75-milliwatt CW lasers: two customers confirmed requirements met electrically; 200 gig per lane photodetector demand strong into calendar 2027

quarterly_data.signal: Capacity and supply: MACOM is adding indium phosphide photodetector manufacturing capacity to keep up with customers' forecasted demand (amount not disclosed for competitive reasons). The North Carolina (RTP) fab has 'a very aggressive plan to increase output by 30%', with some equipment bought and cycle-time reduction as the site's number one priority. Gross margin gains this year and next come mainly from higher utilization of the Massachusetts fab and to some degree the French fab, whose three-inch to six-inch wafer transition is targeted to be fully qualified and released to production by June 2026; one high-mix fab runs GaAs, GaN, silicon and indium phosphide. Benefits from insourcing IPDs and capacitors now bought from a third-party vendor will most likely come in 2027 and beyond. On supply, 'we are absolutely in ramp mode in various programs', and availability of indium phosphide and other exotic materials is a key focus; pricing is rational, and 'we're in an environment where there is scarcity in some areas'. Fiscal 2026 capex is still estimated at $50 million to $55 million (Q1 capex $12.9 million).
quarterly_data.figure: RTP fab plan to increase output by 30%; FY2026 capex $50 million to $55 million; Q1 capex $12.9 million

quarterly_data.signal: Telecom: MACOM's previously announced $55 million satellite contract (with the potential of an additional $25 million add-on) is planned to start production in 2026, delayed mainly by satellite system changes flowed down from the customer, which management views as positive because added functionality should bring new customers to the constellation. MACOM says it is engaged at some level with all of the major LEO constellations (microwave, optics, satellite-to-satellite, direct-to-device and ground stations), has multiple SATCOM LEO programs in design, and expects SATCOM to grow nicely into 2027. In 5G, one competitor is exiting the RF power GaN market; MACOM hired a team of experienced engineers and is sampling next-generation GaN4 products, but expects share gains to take one or two years with a flat RAN market in 2026. Cable TV is expected to be a modest contributor to fiscal 2026 telecom growth.
quarterly_data.figure: $55 million satellite contract (potential additional $25 million add-on); production planned to start in 2026

quarterly_data.signal: Balance sheet and capital: cash, cash equivalents and short-term investments were $768 million, with a net cash position of more than $268 million as of January 2, 2026. MACOM planned to retire its 2021 convertible notes in mid-March by paying $161 million of principal in cash (conversion premium in shares), leaving approximately $340 million of convertible notes maturing in December 2029; share buybacks are 'not something that we're contemplating'. Q1 cash flow from operations was approximately $42.9 million and inventories were $238.9 million. Longer term, CEO Stephen Daly said management doubled the company in about four years and now wants to 'double the size of this company and not take four years', executing a strategic plan 'that gets us to $2 billion with a reasonable CAGR'.

quarterly_data.quarter: Sivers Semiconductors press release: Sivers Semiconductors Invests USD 30 Million to Expand (09-03-2026)
quarterly_data.signal: Sivers announced a USD 30 million investment to expand its Indium Phosphide (InP) manufacturing facility in Glasgow, Scotland, ahead of anticipated customer production ramps driven by AI datacenter and optical networking demand; upon completion the expanded facility is expected to support annual production of more than 100 million CW DFB lasers, adding new process capabilities and increased automation; the program begins in the second half of 2026 and is expected to become operational in the fourth quarter of 2027, complementing foundry, packaging and manufacturing partners in Asia under the Hybrid Manufacturing strategy. CEO Vickram Vathulya: the AI infrastructure build-out is creating unprecedented demand across the optical supply chain and customers need significantly more laser production capacity.

quarterly_data.signal: First half of the fiscal year ending March 2026 (April-September 2025; semi-annual report): net sales JPY 559.0 billion (+24.9% year on year), operating income JPY 90.2 billion (+63.5%), ordinary income JPY 91.7 billion (+75.7%), net income attributable to owners of the parent JPY 67.1 billion (+133.7%). By segment: Information & Communications net sales JPY 303.5 billion (+63.4%) and operating income JPY 73.8 billion (+117.5%), as data-center demand driven by the spread and expansion of generative AI kept growing; Electronics net sales JPY 86.2 billion (-2.4%) and operating income down 55.5%, as the downstream supply-chain problem feared since the start of the year materialised, plus higher costs from the strong baht, delayed productivity improvement on new-model products and intensifying competition; Automotive net sales JPY 86.2 billion (-6.2%) and operating income down 38.0%, still profitable but with lower delivery volumes as order programs reached a changeover period, and soaring material costs; Energy net sales JPY 73.2 billion (+2.2%) and operating income up 52.0% on more shipments of high-margin products and better selling prices; Real Estate (Fukagawa Gatharia rental income) net sales up 2.8%. Group R&D spending in the half was JPY 9.2 billion, with no material change in R&D activities; no material contracts.

quarterly_data.signal: 2028 Mid-Term Business Plan (published May 2026; annual securities report): for the plan's final year, fiscal 2028 (the year starting April 2028), the company targets net sales of JPY 1.6 trillion, operating income of JPY 315.0 billion, ROE of 28.5% and ROIC of 21.6%. The plan shifts from 'defensive' to 'offensive' selection and concentration, accelerating strategic investment in growth fields and concentrating resources on 'information infrastructure' and 'information storage', where data-center demand is expected to keep growing; it also pursues fusion energy. Management expects hyperscale data-center construction and data center interconnect (DCI) investment driven by generative AI to continue, keeping demand for optical wiring solutions at a high level, and expects hyperscale data-center demand centred on North America to keep expanding, with optical fiber cable and multi-fiber optical connector demand staying high; it will strengthen production capacity and supply. From fiscal 2026 (the year starting April 2026) the Electronics and Automotive segments are combined into a new Electronics & Electrical segment.
quarterly_data.figure: Fiscal 2028 (year starting April 2028) targets: net sales JPY 1.6 trillion; operating income JPY 315.0 billion; ROE 28.5%; ROIC 21.6%

quarterly_data.signal: Optical capacity expansion (annual securities report): in March 2026 the company decided to invest up to JPY 300.0 billion in total in Japan and the US to expand optical fiber cable production capacity up to 3 times the current level; under a framework agreement signed with the US Department of Commerce in October 2025, it aims to raise optical fiber and SWR/WTC capacity each to up to 3 times the current level. It invested to raise MT ferrule (a key part of multi-fiber optical connectors) capacity about 1.7 times versus fiscal 2024 (the year starting April 2024) and, with data-center demand still strong, is considering further expansion; it is also increasing MT/MMC ferrule output and strengthening wiring-component capacity at its Vietnam, Mexico and Poland plants. For optical cable, it is investing in WTC production equipment in Morocco, using the Automotive business's Moroccan plant, targeting operation in the first half of fiscal 2026 (April-September 2026), for a recovering European market and expansion in the Middle East and Africa.
quarterly_data.figure: Up to JPY 300.0 billion in Japan and the US; optical fiber cable capacity up to 3x; MT ferrule capacity about 1.7x vs fiscal 2024 (year starting April 2024)

quarterly_data.signal: Capex and plant plans (annual securities report): capital expenditure in the year ended March 2026 totalled JPY 40.3 billion, concentrated on growth fields. At the Sakura Works (Sakura, Chiba) a next-generation optical fiber / SWR plant is under construction for about JPY 45.0 billion. Planned new facilities (Information & Communications): Sakura Works SWR new plant, total JPY 10,077 million (JPY 8,221 million already paid), started August 2023, completion June 2026, capacity increase 1.3 times; Sakura Works SWR new plant, total JPY 44,963 million (JPY 33 million paid), started August 2025, completion in fiscal 2029 (the year starting April 2029), capacity increase about 2 times.
quarterly_data.figure: Capex JPY 40.3 billion; Sakura SWR plant JPY 10,077 million (completion June 2026, 1.3x); Sakura SWR plant JPY 44,963 million (completion fiscal 2029 (year starting April 2029), about 2x)

quarterly_data.signal: Information & Communications products and R&D (annual securities report): in fiscal 2025 (the year ended March 2026) the company began selling what it calls the world's first 13,824-fiber SWR/WTC cable for hyperscale data centers, doubling the previous maximum of 6,912 fibers while keeping the outer diameter at 40 mm or less, and commercialised a 4,000-fiber SWR/WTC for the Japanese data-center market. It increased output of MMC (Miniature Multi-Row Connector) ferrules, which are being adopted in data centers, launched MMC trunk cables using SWR/WTC, and plans further increases in MMC ferrule and MMC trunk cable output. It developed a new multi-fiber fusion splicer, mainly for building generative-AI data centers, with sales planned from fiscal 2026 (the year starting April 2026) (automatic fiber alignment, end-gap correction, GPS logging), and a new core-alignment splicer for low-loss long-haul fiber. Segment R&D spending was JPY 11.5 billion of group R&D of JPY 16.8 billion.
quarterly_data.figure: 13,824-fiber WTC (vs 6,912 previous max), outer diameter 40 mm or less; segment R&D JPY 11.5 billion; group R&D JPY 16.8 billion

quarterly_data.signal: CPO and next-generation fiber (annual securities report): the company's polarization-maintaining fiber is increasingly being adopted for co-packaged optics (CPO), and its CPO shipments increased in fiscal 2025 (the year ended March 2026); it will focus on manufacturing technology to raise productivity and lower cost to meet growing demand. Next-generation optical fiber is a priority R&D area: multicore and hollow-core fiber for thinner diameter and lower loss, and applying PANDA fiber and image fiber technology to contribute to CPO and other opto-electronic integration. It has also developed composite modules integrating fiber couplers for submarine-cable repeaters.
quarterly_data.figure: no specific figure

quarterly_data.signal: Fusion and fiber lasers (annual securities report): high-temperature superconducting wire, used in the superconducting magnets of compact fusion reactors, is being expanded at the Sakura Works; the company decided in fiscal 2025 (the year ended March 2026) on a plant expansion of about JPY 5.6 billion and plans to raise capacity about 3-4 times versus fiscal 2024 (the year starting April 2024) in fiscal 2027 (the year starting April 2027) and about a further 2 times in fiscal 2028 (the year starting April 2028). Its single-mode fiber laser output was raised to 7 kW, it develops pulsed fiber lasers with semiconductor equipment makers for each process step, and it has partnerships with EX-Fusion and Blue Laser Fusion Inc. toward applying fiber lasers to laser fusion.
quarterly_data.figure: HTS wire plant expansion about JPY 5.6 billion; capacity about 3-4x vs fiscal 2024 in fiscal 2027, about 2x more in fiscal 2028 (Japanese fiscal years starting April); 7 kW single-mode fiber laser

quarterly_data.signal: Electronics outlook and data-center products (annual securities report): management expects smartphone demand at major customers, which use many FPCs and connectors, to stay firm, but is watching whether higher handset prices caused by surging memory prices hurt replacement demand; FPC will keep shifting to high-value-added products. For data centers it will strengthen HDD component production and thermal product development: new cold plates with a proprietary structure and higher-performance 3D vapor chambers for higher-heat CPUs/GPUs used in generative AI. Electronics R&D was JPY 2.4 billion. In Automotive, management expects global vehicle production to increase versus fiscal 2025 (the year ended March 2026), while watching US auto tariffs and the slowing EV market.

quarterly_data.signal: SHARE + DESIGN-IN: FiberEdge TIA/driver share at 800G went from ABOUT 18% two years ago to WELL OVER 50% today, and Semtech expects to EXIT FY2027 (January 2027) with BETTER THAN 50% share of 1.6T FiberEdge. Now designed in at EVERY module provider in its target markets, SEVERAL ON A SOLE-SOURCE BASIS, across both fully-retimed and linear architectures. Driver revenue is still ahead of it ('a wonderful product in the evaluation, will be contributing to the revenue very meaningfully'). CopperEdge linear equalizers described as the DE FACTO INDUSTRY STANDARD for ACC — already taking 'the lion's share' of the linear-equalizer market — volume-ready up to 1.6T and in DESIGN-IN AT ALL BANDWIDTHS UP TO 3.2T (1.6T / 2.4T / 3.2T roadmap), on link-margin and power advantages. ACC volume deployment at the lead hyperscaler INFLECTS IN Q4 FY2027 (cable makers already ordering, up QoQ); ACC adoption coincides with NEW PLATFORM designs rather than displacing installed AEC. Broad linear-equalizer-ON-BOARD design activity across multiple hyperscalers, several 'reaching the finish line' near term; interoperability not yet a customer priority (availability first).

quarterly_data.signal: PHOTONICS BUILD-OUT (HieFo acquired ~5-6 months ago, plus a series of photonic acquisitions completed in under six months): portfolio now spans GAIN CHIPS (the one product shipping in volume today), HIGH-POWER CW LASERS, SEMICONDUCTOR OPTICAL AMPLIFIERS (SOA, now sampling) and newly-added HIGH-SPEED PHOTODIODES / PD ARRAYS (design team brought on under an industry leader, to be co-optimized with Semtech's own TIAs). High-power CW laser sampled to FIVE-SIX MODULE MANUFACTURERS with very positive feedback on power-conversion efficiency, beam and over-temperature performance; one CW laser splits into 4 or 8 channels for 1.6T and 3.2T transceivers. Beyond the THREE ANCHOR gain-chip customers (all increasing demand), new key customers have been added now that Semtech stands behind the asset. Timeline: CW laser + SOA available for customer sampling/qualification within ~2 months; CW-LASER-FOR-TRANSCEIVER REVENUE STARTS H1 FY2028. Content per transceiver targeted to rise from HIGH SINGLE-DIGIT DOLLARS to HIGH DOUBLE-DIGIT DOLLARS as the industry moves 800G → 3.2T — CEO explicitly clarified this means $80-90, NOT $18-19 — coinciding with the 3.2T cut-in. CFO: PD and CW laser products carry DATA-CENTER gross margins, ACCRETIVE to the ~64% post-divestiture corporate average.
quarterly_data.figure: Content/transceiver high-single-digit $ → $80-90 at 3.2T; CW laser revenue starts H1 FY2028

quarterly_data.signal: CAPACITY, BACKLOG & PRICING: RECORD BACKLOG — the remainder of FY2027 is 'all booked' and OVER 70% OF FY2028 is already booked. CEO warns the capacity secured MAY NOT BE ENOUGH to support FY2028, ESPECIALLY H2 FY2028, and says there is room in the industry to secure ANOTHER 50-100% of capacity. Actions: acquired an ALREADY FULLY-FACILITIZED FAB in close proximity to the existing photonics site, raising fab capacity 3-4x BY END OF FY2027 (on track); adding BACK-END TESTERS and qualifying ADDITIONAL OSAT partners (test, packaging, die-separation) partly to MITIGATE GEOPOLITICAL RISK; front-end capacity being expanded with a leading partner via PREPAYMENT / CapEx / other means. CapEx was 2% of net sales in Q2 (fab capacity for gain chips and CW lasers) and is expected to grow but stay GENERALLY BELOW 5% of sales. PRICING: 'availability is more important to the customers than the pricing' — NO price erosion expected in the near term and none on orders already in backlog; CFO confirms NO price erosion at 800G. Input costs rising slightly and being PASSED THROUGH to customers.
quarterly_data.figure: >70% of FY2028 booked; fab capacity 3-4x by end FY2027; room for +50-100% capacity; no price erosion

quarterly_data.signal: MARKET / ROADMAP DATA POINTS: 800G transceiver INDUSTRY volume went from ~20 MILLION UNITS/YEAR two years ago to ~90 MILLION UNITS/YEAR this year — the industry entered the year forecasting 50M units and Semtech is 'now hearing the number 80, 90 million'; 800G bookings are still INCREASING (not decreasing), and 800G and 1.6T both have 'a really very healthy runway over the next two years'. 3.2T TIMING: design window starts opening in ~12 MONTHS, EARLY MOVERS ~18 MONTHS OUT, MEANINGFUL DEPLOYMENT IN ~2 YEARS (i.e. H2 CY2028) — that is the cut-in for Semtech's content step-up, and above 200G/lane is where TIA + photodiode CO-OPTIMIZATION becomes necessary. MPO/NPO called a strong trend driven by BANDWIDTH-DENSITY limits against fixed shoreline: Semtech is engaged on '10, 15 DIFFERENT PROGRAMS' with module manufacturers, some tied directly to end customers, as a leading supplier of TIA ARRAYS and (linearized) LASER ARRAYS; higher density tightens element spacing and crosstalk, changing packaging requirements. LPO has generated meaningful revenue since Q1 FY2027 and is growing moderately, but its bigger effect is PROVING THE LINEAR ARCHITECTURE, which now carries into MPO, XPO and 'some form of CPO'. Stated R&D priority: lasers, photodiodes, drivers and TIAs for 3.2T coherent light, XPO, MPO and CPO applications. Analyst day 10-15-2026 (San Jose) will publish TAM, share and the multi-year model.
quarterly_data.figure: 800G industry units ~20M/yr (2024) → ~90M/yr (2026); 3.2T volume ~2 years out; 10-15 MPO/NPO programs

quarterly_data.signal: LASER ACQUISITION: Semtech acquired HIFU Corporation (name as printed in this transcript), a California-based maker of indium phosphide optoelectronic devices (gain chips and CW laser chips for optical transceivers), with a comprehensive investment plan for the Alhambra, California facility. Combining its InP lasers with Semtech's TIAs and laser drivers raises Semtech's content opportunity 'from high single-digit dollars in an 800G module to about $80 in a 3.2T module'. The fab is vertically integrated (epi growth, multi-step regrowth, wafer processing, internal test; backend packaging via the ecosystem). The gain chip for tunable lasers is in volume production, capacity limited, and should contribute 'roughly about a high-teen level of revenue' in fiscal 2027. The CW laser for transceivers has 42% wall-plug efficiency at room temperature vs a typical about 25%; there is not enough capacity for industry demand, multiple customers asked for samples, and Semtech plans to intercept at 3.2T transceivers (1.6T also supported). Go-to-market: co-optimized chipsets (TIA, laser driver, modulator driver + lasers) with a reference design; 'the major inflection point is 3.2T transceiver modules. It could be earlier than that.' Deal expected to be accretive to non-GAAP EPS within the first year.
quarterly_data.figure: content from high single-digit dollars (800G) to about $80 in a 3.2T module; CW laser wall-plug efficiency 42% vs about 25% typical

quarterly_data.signal: CAPACITY: FY2027 priority is supporting customer ramps 'as we compete in a capacity-constrained environment'. CFO: the CapEx should qualify for the Section 48 investment tax credit of 35%, plus other government grant programs. Copper linear equalizers onboard have multiple customer engagements, with customers defining five or six use cases (switch, merchant GPU board, hyperscaler ASIC board, active backplane); qualification expected within the coming quarters. OFC demos: 1.6T ACCs running live traffic to NVIDIA's 224G SerDes and next-generation 448G per-channel CopperEdge chips.

NPO is a complement to CPO that leverages the whole ecosystem: 'In CPO, we may not have much content in there except for lasers. quarterly_data.quarter: Semtech press release: Semtech Advances Next-Gen AI Optical Interconnects for XPO (09-21-2026)
quarterly_data.signal: Semtech announced its membership in the eXtra-dense Pluggable Optics MSA as a technology partner and detailed its 200G/lane XPO product family of linear modulator drivers and TIAs: GN1834L and GN1834DL quad TIAs, GN1838L and GN1838DL octal TIAs, the GN42T380 octal TIA, TN1877 quad and TN1887 octal Mach-Zehnder Modulator (MZM) drivers, and the GN42M380 octal MZM driver, with on-chip equalization, integrated telemetry and ultra-low latency for high-density AI network switch and fabric applications. Semtech says the portfolio is designed to support XPO 'from early prototyping through volume deployment'; no sampling or availability dates are stated, and the parts are to be demonstrated at ECOC 2026. Per the release, the current XPO generation delivers 12.8T per module at 200G/lane using an integrated liquid-cooling design, with an MSA roadmap to a future generation based on 400G/lane electrical interfaces.
quarterly_data.figure: 200G/lane XPO driver/TIA family; XPO 12.8T per module at 200G/lane, roadmap to 400G/lane

quarterly_data.quarter: Semtech press release: Semtech Enables 50G Optical Transition for AI-Driven (09-21-2026)
quarterly_data.signal: Semtech announced full production availability of its mobile transport portfolio for 50G fronthaul in 5G-Advanced radio deployments, now shipping in volume: GN2255 CDR with the GN1700TI TIA for 10 km duplex links, GN2255S CDR with the GN1700TI TIA for 15 km bidirectional (BiDi) links, and GN2256 CDR with the GN1700TI TIA for WDM and longer-reach architectures. The portfolio is built on its ClearEdge, Tri-Edge and FiberEdge product families and is designed to scale toward 6G through 2030. Source Photonics CTO Frank Chang is quoted saying Semtech's CDR and TIA portfolio gives it the flexibility and performance it needs across the fronthaul architectures its customers deploy. The release cites Ericsson's and Nokia's new radios as the industry's move to 50G interfaces (they are not stated to be Semtech customers). No revenue or unit figures stated.
quarterly_data.figure: 50G fronthaul CDR/TIA portfolio in full production (10 km duplex, 15 km BiDi, WDM links)

quarterly_data.quarter: Semtech press release: Semtech Sets Bar for 224G Optical Connectivity (09-09-2026)
quarterly_data.signal: Semtech introduced a family of 224G linear TIA and driver solutions designed for Near-Packaged Optics (NPO) and Co-Packaged Optics (CPO) architectures for AI/ML clusters and hyperscale data centers: the GN1838L and GN42T380 linear octal TIAs (which Semtech calls the industry's first linear octal TIAs) and the GN42M380 linear octal Mach-Zehnder Modulator (MZM) driver, optimized for 1.6T, 3.2T, 6.4T and 12.8T optical engines and for CEI-224G-Linear and Open CPX interfaces. The GN1838L offers a 500µm channel pitch and the GN42T380 a 375µm channel pitch; the TIAs can be placed side-by-side with the photonics integrated circuit (PIC) or directly on top of it. The GN42M380 driver (375µm channel pitch) supports silicon photonics, indium phosphide MZM and thin-film lithium niobate modulators. No availability date is stated (the release says to contact Semtech for availability). Amit Thakar, VP signal integrity product marketing: the TIAs and drivers are 'purpose-built to give NPO and CPO developers the building blocks to scale optical I/O while addressing the power and density challenges of next-generation AI systems.'
quarterly_data.figure: 224G per lane; octal TIAs at 500µm and 375µm channel pitch; for 1.6T, 3.2T, 6.4T and 12.8T optical engines

quarterly_data.signal: CEO Seamus Grady walked the capacity ladder to a single consolidated number: capacity right now is about $5.8 billion (the $5.3 billion Q4 exit run rate plus the Pinehurst office-to-manufacturing conversion); Building 10 when fully available adds about $3.5 billion at the high end; Nava, the new factory in Nava Nakorn, adds about $250 million; and the newly acquired Santa Clara operation adds about another $250 million - which gets to $9.8 billion of capacity in calendar Q1, early in the March quarter, an 85% increase versus where the year ended. Beyond that, Building 11 - not yet announced - would take probably 18 months to build and add capacity for another $2.1 billion approximately, and the same for Building 12, so over the next three years Fabrinet could add another $4.2 billion on top of the $9.8 billion, taking it to approximately $14 billion of capacity. quarterly_data.signal: Grady quantified the build-ahead economics of Building 10: it is about a 2 million sq ft factory costing about $132 million, $133 million for the building, and even if it were to sit idle the gross margin headwind is about 15 basis points, while just over five months' worth of operating profit at full run rate would pay for the whole factory. It will not sit idle - Fabrinet is already installing equipment and getting going on Floor 1 and will start to occupy Floor 3 in October. 'The downside risk is tiny and the upside opportunity is immense', with the real downside being that if the capacity is not put in place customers have to go somewhere else. Fit-out follows the customer: generic or standard equipment is paid for by Fabrinet, product-specific or unique equipment is paid for by the customer.

Fabrinet took a small $75 million term loan signed with a Thai bank in August to finance growth in Thailand and is expanding credit lines, but is very comfortable with the balance sheet and comfortable financing growth from its own free cash flow rather than equity, because return on invested capital is close to the 40% mark. quarterly_data.signal: Datacom diversification status: Fabrinet is actually shipping to both hyperscale-direct and merchant transceiver manufacturers right now, and it is early days. The non-NVIDIA datacom customers are mostly initially 800 gig short reach transceivers and then moving to 1.6 in the future, with the initial foray at 800 gig. Grady reiterated Fabrinet will never become an ODM or own the IP - companies like Ciena, Cisco and Nokia would be deeply upset if it became a product company - and said Fabrinet has been picking up and winning business with some customers precisely because some competitors chose the ODM route. Management said it does not overly analyse share (customers do not always disclose it) and focuses instead on growing each opportunity to the multi-$100 million level where it can properly resource the customer. Beyond hyperscale, Fabrinet is also working with quantum compute customers that would fall into the new data center category, because moving those workloads around will need optics and not just electronics.

quarterly_data.signal: First margin math on NPO/CPO: on a typical product, if COGS is 100%, roughly 70%-80% is material and 20% is value add. For NPO the material content is much lower - in many cases the wafer is consigned by the customer and Fabrinet singulates it, does the packaging and the testing at die and device level - so it is much higher value add, probably a lower ASP but a higher margin, and Grady said NPO 'would be much better gross margin than our traditional business'. He cautioned the business needs a mix of both higher-volume lower-margin work and this higher-margin lower-ASP work, and described NPO as probably a little bit more straightforward than CPO, with the opportunity in NPO extending well beyond ELSFPs to the packaging of the devices themselves.

quarterly_data.signal: OCS ramp timing put on the clock for the first time: Fabrinet has shipped some OCS product but it is quite small today, and is working with a number of companies, one of whom it is actually shipping product to, while the others are early days and more startup-type companies. Management is looking forward to really beginning to ramp that over the next 12 to 18 months. On Coherent specifically, Grady said Coherent has a lot of its own in-house capacity at both the system level and the wafer level and does a lot of the in-house silicon itself, so he believes Coherent will continue to manufacture in-house. quarterly_data.quarter: Accelink press release: Accelink 12.8T XPO DR Liquid-Cooling Real-World Test: See (09-18-2026)
quarterly_data.signal: Accelink's 12.8T XPO DR liquid-cooled pluggable optical module (on display at its ECOC 2026 booth #1007) adopts the LRO linear receive architecture with a 64x200G PAM4 design: a single module delivers 12.8T bps, equivalent to eight 1.6T modules, in a pluggable package only 2.7 times the width of a traditional OSFP module. For 204.8T of switching capacity a traditional 1.6T OSFP solution needs 4U of rack space versus 1U for the 12.8T XPO solution (front-panel bandwidth density up to four times higher), aimed at high-density AI cluster scale-out and scale-up networks. LRO cuts power consumption by 30% versus a Full DSP solution; a built-in integrated cold plate removes heat from the DSP and optical engine, and quick-disconnect liquid-cooling interfaces allow on-site front-panel module replacement. The XPO platform supports LPO, LRO, FRO and other interface architectures and DR, FR, LR, ZR/ZR+ optical interface standards. Shown as an exhibit; no availability date, customers or volumes stated.
quarterly_data.figure: 12.8T per module (64x200G PAM4, 2.7 times OSFP width); 204.8T switching in 1U vs 4U; 30% lower power vs Full DSP

quarterly_data.signal: Accelink says it has launched an 800G L Band OSFP ZR/ZR+ pluggable coherent module, debuted in China with a live demo at CIOE 2026. It uses Accelink's self-developed L-Band optical devices (the company says it designs and manufactures the chain from the coherent optical engine to key optical components in-house) and achieves L-Band output power better than 0 dBm in a compact OSFP package; the company says the module has stable mass-production capability. Used in parallel with C-band, it supports single-fiber capacity doubling from 25.6T to 51.2T without new fiber, and complies with OIF 800ZR, OpenZR+ and OpenROADM. Target uses: cloud data center DCI, metro backbone and campus computing networks. No customers, volumes or availability date stated.

quarterly_data.quarter: Accelink press release: From 3.2T to 6.4T NPO: Accelink Redefines the "Optical (09-04-2026)
quarterly_data.signal: Accelink released a new-generation 6.4T NPO (near-packaged optics) optical engine, debuted at CIOE 2026 for next-generation AI scenarios. Design: a transceiver-integrated silicon photonic PIC supporting 32x200G parallel channels, a linear direct-drive EIC, 2.5D Flip-Chip packaging with multi-channel fiber-array optical coupling, and a pluggable Socket interface; the OE optical engine is paired with an ELSFP external light source and an FMU-Shuffle fiber management unit as an end-to-end NPO solution. The company says this follows what it calls the industry's first full-system verification of a 3.2T silicon photonic single-mode NPO in March 2026, and argues NPO is a more balanced path than CPO because it keeps short electrical links and low power while staying maintainable and drawing on the mature optical-module supply chain. Exhibit only; no customers, volumes or availability date stated.

Its key foundry partners are Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Corporation (TSMC) in Taiwan and United Microelectronics Corporation (UMC) in Taiwan and Singapore; a large portion of its products are manufactured by TSMC and UMC, and it has no long-term supply contracts with most of its vendors, including TSMC and UMC, buying substantially all on a purchase order basis. Certain products are supplied by Intel Corporation on a turnkey basis, and the majority of its assembly/packaging and test is done by Advanced Semiconductor Engineering (ASE), Greatek Electronics, Signetics Corporation, SIGURD Microelectronics and Silicon Precision Industries. It gives foundry and assembly/test contractors production forecasts six to twelve months in advance, places firm orders up to twenty-six weeks before delivery, and had inventory purchase obligations of $168,484 thousand as of December 31, 2025 ($117,910 thousand due in 2026 and $50,574 thousand in 2027).

quarterly_data.signal: Chairman Gerald G Wong: silicon-photonics modules scale up more easily than traditional EML designs; at 100G/lane (800G) the two are at parity, at 200G/lane (1.6T) silicon photonics has the edge, and at 400G/lane EML currently leads because of silicon-modulator bandwidth limits. Thin-film lithium niobate could improve modulator performance and the company is investing via capital and technical partnerships; management said a pure thin-film lithium niobate design will not work for 3.2T/400G and an integrated design is required. External-light-source NPO is a clear future direction. The company started silicon-photonics R&D six years ago and commercialised it three years ago.

quarterly_data.signal: Fiscal Q4 2026 record quarter (CEO Sam Rubin, CFO Albert Miranda): revenue $21.2 million, up 73% from $12.2 million in the year-ago quarter - a company record and the fourth consecutive quarter of sequential growth. By product group: infrared components $7.1 million (34% of revenue), visible components $4.2 million (20%), assemblies and modules $9.1 million (43%), engineering services $800 thousand (4%). Gross profit rose 210% to $8.3 million, a 39.4% gross margin vs 22% a year earlier; adjusted EBITDA $2.1 million (10% of revenue) vs an adjusted EBITDA loss of $2.0 million, the fourth consecutive quarter of positive adjusted EBITDA; net loss $4.1 million ($0.06 per share) vs $7.1 million ($0.16 per share).
quarterly_data.figure: Q4 revenue $21.2 million (+73% YoY); gross margin 39.4% (22% a year earlier); adjusted EBITDA $2.1 million (10% of revenue); net loss $4.1 million

quarterly_data.signal: Fiscal 2026 full year (CFO Albert Miranda): revenue up 93% to $71.7 million from $37.2 million in fiscal 2025 - infrared components $21.2 million (30% of revenue, up 52%), visible components $15.5 million (22%, up 32%), assemblies and modules $31.9 million (44%, up 281%), engineering services $3.1 million (4%, roughly flat). Gross margin expanded from 27% to 36%; adjusted EBITDA was a $4.2 million profit vs a $5.1 million loss in fiscal 2025, a swing of $9.3 million. CEO Sam Rubin: assemblies, modules and cameras were 43% of Q4 and 44% of the full year vs 23% of revenue in fiscal 2025; the 39.4% Q4 margin 'did not come from a one-time favorable contract or from raising prices' but from that mix (higher prices and margins than the legacy component business) and from execution - past yield and throughput problems in components are 'in the past', and every one of the four product groups improved its margin year over year. CFO: the margin also reflected better absorption on higher volume and a $5 million inventory reserve charge in the prior year that did not recur. Year-end cash was $93.2 million with effectively no debt.
quarterly_data.figure: FY2026 revenue $71.7 million (+93% from $37.2 million); gross margin 36% (27% in FY2025); adjusted EBITDA $4.2 million (loss of $5.1 million in FY2025); cash $93.2 million

quarterly_data.signal: CFO Albert Miranda on costs: Q4 operating expenses were $12.6 million vs $7.2 million a year earlier; $2.0 million of the increase was a noncash fair-value adjustment to acquisition earn-out liabilities, primarily G5 Infrared reflecting its strong performance against the earn-out targets, and the remaining $3.4 million was mainly SG&A (the addition of AMI operations, incentive compensation accruals, senior leadership additions, higher sales and marketing, IT spend to meet customer security requirements). Fiscal 2026 operating expenses were $45.5 million vs $22.0 million, including $14.1 million of noncash earn-out fair-value adjustment; new product development costs also increased. The $15.6 million fiscal 2026 earn-out charge remeasures what the G5 sellers earned because G5 is outperforming the estimate made at acquisition; the final G5 earn-out was agreed and accrued in Q4 for payment in January 2027, with possible small future adjustments related to AMI and Visimid.
quarterly_data.figure: Q4 opex $12.6 million (incl. $2.0 million earn-out adjustment); FY2026 opex $45.5 million (incl. $14.1 million earn-out adjustment); FY2026 earn-out charge $15.6 million

quarterly_data.signal: Backlog at June 30 was $110.9 million, up 197% from $37.4 million a year earlier, with approximately $85.6 million requested by customers for delivery within 12 months (CFO Albert Miranda). CEO Sam Rubin: backlog did not grow sequentially in Q4, but shortly after quarter-end the company reported two large orders totaling $24 million (July) and has kept booking, so the next quarter's backlog will already show more growth. The two July orders are for 2027 delivery, already in production and on a cadence of deliveries spread over months, and are expected to be renewed in the years to come as programs of record typically are; much of the current ordering is for production as programs move from qualification to production. By application, counter-UAS is 'still probably one of the biggest parts of the backlog', optics for drones and assemblies for drone dominance are a growing part, and there is not a lot of border patrol in it yet.
quarterly_data.figure: Backlog $110.9 million (+197% from $37.4 million); ~$85.6 million for delivery within 12 months; two July orders totaling $24 million

quarterly_data.signal: CEO Sam Rubin: capacity is the single biggest operational theme for fiscal 2027 and glass is 'by far' the biggest capacity constraint - demand for glass is running ahead of supply even after the January acquisition of Amorphous Materials (AMI), which increased BlackDiamond melting capacity and unlocked large-diameter melting up to 10 inches and beyond vs the 5 inches produced before (large diameter opens long-range camera systems, large assemblies and space-based missile detection and tracking); doubling glass capacity was 'nowhere near enough'. LightPath is adding melting capacity in Orlando and Texas (and will probably need even more), moving AMI's operations into a larger building near its Visimid camera business in the Dallas area, and expanding optical fabrication, coating and assembly across its U.S. and Latvian sites, adding shifts in all locations. After glass, detectors are the long pole: lead times have grown from about six months to ten months or more, so the company is building inventory ahead; mechanics, motors (magnets) and other components have also become material constraints.
quarterly_data.figure: Large-diameter glass melting up to 10 inches (vs 5 inches before); detector lead times from about six months to ten months or more

quarterly_data.signal: Capex was $6.3 million in fiscal 2026, $4.4 million of it in Q4 - the last time LightPath spent at that level was calendar 2023, when it expanded the Orlando facility and doubled the clean room (CFO Albert Miranda). Fiscal 2027 capex will be higher than fiscal 2026, 'a deliberate choice made against a visible order book and pipeline' (CEO Sam Rubin); CFO: all locations will be expanded to meet the backlog and the demand foreseen through fiscal 2027 and into fiscal 2028, getting ahead of demand in key areas like BlackDiamond glass production. CEO on fiscal 2027: 'less about proving the thesis and more about scaling against it. Doubling a manufacturing business in 12 months is hard. Doing it twice in a row is harder, and it will require capacity we are still building and people we are still hiring.' CFO: the fiscal 2027 mandate is to add capacity fast enough, hold the margin gains and convert the book, and it is 'fully funded'. CEO: the company will also pursue accretive, capability-adding acquisitions similar to G5 and AMI.
quarterly_data.figure: FY2026 capex $6.3 million ($4.4 million in Q4); FY2027 capex to be higher than FY2026

quarterly_data.signal: CEO Sam Rubin on germanium substitution: China's first restrictions on germanium and gallium exports in late 2024 started a growth in demand for BlackDiamond glass and systems using it; redesigns to BlackDiamond and new programs - whose design and qualification can take up to two years - are now beginning to move into production, and much of the recent backlog and bookings growth comes from them. He expects the trend to intensify because most customers did not start their redesign and substitution effort until well after the initial germanium export ban; new customers are being won both by converting them to BlackDiamond and by supplying assemblies and systems. LightPath has two domestic glass plants and, in his words, 'the broadest portfolio of infrared materials available'. On germanium supply he now sees more runway than he first thought: one of the leading companies noted current production of only three to four tons per year with increases several years out, and U.S. mining or refining awards also talk about single-digit tons, so he does not see new capacity solving the whole problem in the near term.
quarterly_data.figure: Design and qualification up to two years; germanium production of only three to four tons per year at one of the leading companies

quarterly_data.signal: China exit (CEO Sam Rubin): in July LightPath signed a definitive agreement to sell its China subsidiary to an entity owned by the local management team that ran the facility, expected to close 'later this month'. Roughly $1.5 million of annual third-party revenue leaves the consolidated results; the entity will keep supplying LightPath as a third-party vendor for its commercial customers in the U.S. and Europe, so there is no disruption to them. LightPath now melts glass, coats optics and builds cameras and assemblies exclusively outside China - in Orlando, Plano (Texas), Hudson (New Hampshire) and Riga (Latvia) - with no ownership, facility or commercial activity in China; six years ago most of its manufacturing was in China and more than a third of revenue came from China. CEO: for a customer base now dominated by defense primes and public safety agencies, this opens significant bid opportunities where it is a condition for participation. Defense programs must move optical glass and optical component sourcing from covered nations before the end of the decade; with two-to-three-year qualification cycles, the sourcing decisions for 2029 and 2030 are being made now, and executive orders on germanium waivers, critical-material classification and tariffs would likely pull the timeline closer.
quarterly_data.figure: Roughly $1.5 million of annual third-party revenue leaves with the China subsidiary

quarterly_data.signal: NGSRI, LightPath's three-year-old interceptor program with Lockheed Martin (CEO Sam Rubin): the Army has pushed out the timeline by a few months to potentially explore other options; he sees a delay, not a risk - the new missiles must be reverse-compatible with the tens of thousands of fielded Stinger launchers, primes such as Lockheed and Raytheon have worked on it for three years, and it is 'highly unlikely' that someone else has an equally mature solution in a short time frame. The full qualification of LightPath's low-cost seeker, completed as a result of the NGSRI flight test, opens the door to other opportunities: its camera systems are now designed into or actively evaluated in seven different platforms, three of them with Lockheed Martin and the rest with primes or newer defense entrants ('neoprimes'), all supported from the same Texas manufacturing facility. The seeker groups were relocated into a new building and LightPath has begun investing in seeker-building capacity so a program moving into production can scale quickly. CEO: there is a big push to refill inventories of interceptors like THAAD and Patriot PAC-3 and likely a bigger push for next-generation interceptors; LightPath is involved in many interceptor and precision-munition types but gave no specific numbers.
quarterly_data.figure: Camera systems designed into or evaluated in seven platforms, three with Lockheed Martin

quarterly_data.signal: CEO Sam Rubin on other defense programs: in border tower programs DHS has released funding to the prime, but it has not yet turned into camera orders; demand is growing instead for similar towers and cameras installed outside the U.S., primarily in the Middle East - mostly foreign military sales to allies for border towers in Middle East or North African countries, where LightPath is typically one step down with subprimes and each deal is usually 'in the tens of millions of dollars' for it. Air Force and Army opportunities are mainly counter-UAS and ISR systems. An unnamed airborne program has completed qualification and awaits the LRIP production order; the Apache program may make a comeback with renewed interest. Drone and drone-dominance programs are generating significant demand, which LightPath is meeting by adding automation for high-volume assemblies; two counter-UAS programs are transitioning to a cadence of deliveries of tens of systems a month. SPEIR cameras for the Navy: the first camera, or maybe two, have shipped and he believes another five are in dispatch, expected to ship in the next few weeks.
quarterly_data.figure: Border tower deals usually tens of millions of dollars each; counter-UAS deliveries of tens of systems a month; five more SPEIR cameras in dispatch

quarterly_data.signal: New products, all using BlackDiamond glass instead of germanium (CEO Sam Rubin): the redesign of the last G5 cooled cameras with BlackDiamond is progressing well technically but is behind schedule, and results so far indicate the cameras will work at least as well as the germanium-based ones; the delay reflects stretched supply chains (especially detectors, plus mechanics, other lenses and component changes) and Amorphous melting that glass at that size at scale for one of the first times, which needs fine-tuning. In long-wave infrared (uncooled) cameras, a year-long effort on zoom lenses and zoom cameras is coming to fruition, with the first orders for zoom lenses and complete uncooled zoom cameras to be delivered soon; once fully production-ready he expects market need to translate into orders fairly quickly.

quarterly_data.signal: CALL — GUIDE RAISED A THIRD TIME; SUPPLY CHAIN REBUILT: FY2026 revenue raised to ~$12.6B = 40% GROWTH (+$2.1B vs the $10.5B Analyst Day plan, +$1.1B vs May's $11.5B) — the raise deliberately UNALLOCATED across AI fabrics (goal >=$3.5B), campus (>=$1.25B), core front-end data center ('isn't going to be flat' — enterprise, new logos, international) and routing; operating margin RAISED to 48-49% (Q2 hit 49.9%). Supply chain: Jayshree — 'the INDUSTRY is going to have a TWO-YEAR problem... I don't think we get out of it as an industry TILL 2028,' but Arista's specific H1 actions pay off in H2: MULTI-YEAR PURCHASE COMMITMENTS NEARLY TRIPLED YoY to $9.7 BILLION (from $3.6B; $8.9B in Q1); MEMORY SUPPLY SECURED FOR 2026 with visibility WELL INTO 2027 (DDR4/DDR5/NAND); PCB + optics capacity buildable in a 12-month window; a NEW LIQUID-COOLING SUPPLY CHAIN stood up (cold plates, quick disconnects, tubing with capacity agreements); 3 CMs + 3 distribution hubs (US/Asia/Mexico). Guidance is explicitly supply-gated: 'guiding based on what we're CONFIDENT we can get the supply for — if supply released more, there is opportunity to do better.' Price increases only help 'end of the year or more like next year' (backlog); FY GM held 62-64% including memory/silicon cost inflation. Etherlink AI-fabric customers now EXCEED 100 CUMULATIVE (from 4-5 in 2024).
quarterly_data.figure: FY26 raised to ~$12.6B (+40%, 3rd raise); purchase commitments ~3x YoY to $9.7B; memory secured into 2027; liquid-cooling chain built; >100 AI customers

quarterly_data.signal: CALL — OPEN CPO STANCE AND THE SCALE-UP VIEW: scale-up philosophy = 'COPPER IF YOU CAN, OPTICS IF YOU MUST.' Arista rejects the ~5 proprietary CPO implementations circulating and is committing to ONE OPEN CPO — socketed optical engines, pigtail fibers, fully pre-tested modules, a truly open multi-vendor interface (often called NPO) — with trials/examples NEXT YEAR; 'the MAJORITY of the world will still remain PLUGGABLE OPTICS AND COPPER; there will be SOME co-packaged optics in 2028 and 2029.' Scale-up positioning: 'we live in an NVIDIA world' — where NVIDIA supplies the full NVLink vertical stack there is little Arista participation (Arista wins scale-out/across), but for NON-NVIDIA accelerators (AMD MI series, Google TPUs — 'increasingly a FORMIDABLE training processor', in-house XPUs, inference chips) Arista works BOTH scale-up and scale-out, including CUSTOM RACKS tuned to customers' engines; 'feels like InfiniBand 2-3 years ago... it will take time to move from proprietary NVLink to alternatives, even if Ethernet's really good — I expect us to do much better there.' 1.6T cadence (history repeats 800G's trials-2023/24 -> ramp-2025/26): TRIALS H2 2026 with single-digit VERY LARGE customers; REAL PRODUCTION 2027 (liquid-cooling infrastructure required). EOS innovations for AI fabrics: SSU hitless upgrades, MRC packet-spray/reassembly (kills hash-collision slowdowns), SRv6 explicit-path load balancing with real-time congestion signals — one binary from scale-out to scale-across.
quarterly_data.figure: Open CPO (socketed/NPO) trials 2027; majority stays pluggable+copper, some CPO 2028-29; non-NVIDIA scale-up = the opening (InfiniBand analogy); 1.6T production 2027

quarterly_data.signal: PURCHASE COMMITMENT TRAJECTORY AND WHERE THE TIGHTNESS SITS: CFO Chantelle Breithaupt said purchase commitments were about $3.6 billion three quarters ago and $9.6 billion at the end of Q2 - basically tripling - and that this balance is already covering the second half of next year, since chips carry a year lead time going into Q3 next year. The structural pressure is at the top of fab capacity; Arista found vendor arrangements on fab capacity and memory that it says sorted 2026 and 2027, but peripheral parts (PCBs, capacitors) remain Whac-A-Mole and 'I don't think anyone's out of the woods when it comes to the full supply chain for networking data centers generally'.
quarterly_data.figure: about $3.6 billion; $9.6 billion at the end of Q2; a year lead time for chips going into Q3 next year

quarterly_data.signal: XPO / NPO / CPO ROADMAP WITH DATES: SVP Cloud and AI Networking Tyson Lamoreaux said 'XPO early deployments second half of next year, really ramping in 2028, and probably 12 months behind that is where we start to see some of that CPO ramp occur'. The sequence is copper as long as possible, then NPO/XPO (XPO is the NPO-based architecture) for the multi-rack density copper cannot reach, then CPO once it can be built at scale - early CPO adoption expected, but a completely different manufacturing technology whose yields will be very challenging early on. Arista builds CPO or NPO switches when customers ask; XPO timing is partly aligned with scale-up form factor and bandwidth density needs.
quarterly_data.figure: XPO early deployments second half of next year, really ramping in 2028, and probably 12 months behind that

quarterly_data.signal: SCALE-UP IS ZERO TODAY: Breithaupt said there is 'zero in our guidance and zero revenue for Arista for scale up in 2026', with trials and pilots expected later next year once the Ethernet ecosystem comes together, and '2028 is when we get the revenue there'. Framework: scale-up splits into proprietary (NVLink and UALink), a commodity white-box play for lower value-add needs, and value-add Ethernet where Arista plays - with the open question being how much of the TAM Ethernet starts at and whether proprietary migrates to Ethernet as InfiniBand did. Lamoreaux argued the feature set is smaller in scale-up but reliability, security and telemetry still decide it.
quarterly_data.figure: zero in our guidance and zero revenue for Arista for scale up in 2026; 2028 is when we get the revenue there

quarterly_data.signal: TAM REVISION COMING: Breithaupt said the $105 billion TAM given at the October 2025 Analyst Day is being revisited for scale-up and scale-across because a lot has changed in under a year, with a revised TAM to be presented 'later this year'. She expects it to expand.

quarterly_data.signal: A NEW SCALE-ACROSS DRIVER - POWER POLICY, NOT JUST POWER SCARCITY: Lamoreaux said regulatory regimes and top-down government initiatives are becoming a distinct scale-across driver, citing South Korea, where policy is pushing distributed generation and local consumption of power. The consequence is that data center capacity federates around the country instead of concentrating, each site is capped by locally available power, and those clusters must be interconnected - which he said can shift the scale-across TAM quite a lot.

Supply is still not unconstrained going into next year (described as whack-a-mole), and she said that with a bit more supply Arista could beat even the raised FY2026 guide.

quarterly_data.signal: SCALE-UP ETHERNET (ESAN) SIZING AND POSITION: Gibbs cited an industry analyst report marking Ethernet scale-up networking as high as a $20 billion market by 2030, and said one of Arista's software architects co-chairs the ESAN Network working group at OCP. Breithaupt confirmed Arista has no scale-up product yet ('we do not even have a scale-up offering yet', and none of it sits in deferred revenue), that it will not be material in 2027 financials because standards, pilots and trials come first, and that scale-up will segment into proprietary NVLink, a white-box equivalent, and value-add Ethernet where Arista intends to play.
quarterly_data.figure: a $20 billion market just for Ethernet scale-up networking by 2030; will not be material in our 2027 financials; once it gets going in 2028

quarterly_data.signal: 1.6T TIMING: Gibbs said 1.6T trials are going on now with volume next year, that both air-cooled and liquid-cooled 1.6T systems are announced so liquid cooling is not a gating item (compute nodes drive the liquid-cooling decision, not the network), and that 1.6T ZR optics for scale-across arrive probably next year. Arista is offering XPO (pluggable, liquid-cooled, supports short-range, LPO and ZR+ lasers) alongside open CPO so customers are not locked into one optical approach.
quarterly_data.figure: trials are going on now, volume for next year; 1.6T ZR for scale across probably next year

quarterly_data.signal: DEFERRED REVENUE CONVERSION IS GATED BY DATA CENTER READINESS: CFO Chantelle Breithaupt said product deferred revenue is already shipped, invoiced and usually cash-collected, and converts only on customer acceptance - which can take 18 to 24 months because of power, cooling, facilities and cabling readiness. She gave a live example of a large customer whose data center construction stopped for a three to four-week delay after an employee injury. Deferred revenue today is the new use cases: scale-out, scale-across, eventually scale-up, 800G and 1.6T.
quarterly_data.figure: 18 to 24 months; three to four-week delay

quarterly_data.signal: PRICE INCREASE MECHANICS AND A TARIFF TAILWIND INSIDE THE MARGIN GUIDE: Breithaupt said the single FY2026 price increase was curated, not blanket - applied only to future POs of customers whose bill of material carried a significant component, where 'the largest component is the memory' - and was sized to hold, not accrete, gross margin. It was applied 'only to POs in the future', so the increases land only as backlog works through into new purchase orders. Inside the 62-64 gross margin guide, roughly 30 basis points on the year is a one-time tariff refund flowing back into the P&L. She would not commit to whether a second price increase is needed in 2027.
quarterly_data.figure: 30 basis points; 62-64 guide; the largest component is the memory

quarterly_data.signal: NEOCLOUD CREDIT DISCIPLINE (NOT DISCUSSED ON THE CALL): Breithaupt described NeoClouds as 'almost like a high-risk, high-reward segment', said the segment is not always proven out from a financial backing perspective, and that Arista therefore either walks away from the deal or uses prepayment scenarios - being explicit about where the invoice gets paid, because many NeoClouds start and not all make it. Duda added NeoClouds are an ideal Arista customer because their mandate is lowest token cost, which pushes them to best-of-breed rather than single-vendor lock-in.
quarterly_data.figure: no specific figure

quarterly_data.signal: Deferred revenue year-end outlook: CFO Chantelle Breithaupt said she does not guide deferred and it can come up or down in any quarter, but 'I anticipate deferred to end at a higher balance in Q4 this year than it did Q4 last year', generally going up on the year and complementary to the P&L growth.
quarterly_data.figure: deferred to end at a higher balance in Q4 this year than it did Q4 last year

quarterly_data.signal: Where the silicon constraint sits and how it shapes competition: President and CTO Ken Duda said merchant versus in-house silicon 'isn’t actually the big issue because the bottleneck isn’t the chip designer, the bottleneck is the fab', and that Arista manages allocation through aggressive supply agreements and purchase commitments. He added that 'you do not necessarily get your fair share of the allocation unless you buy the vendor’s turnkey solution' (vendor not named), which pushes lower-volume customers that lack purchase leverage toward a single-vendor solution, while at-scale customers pursue best-of-breed.
quarterly_data.figure: no specific figure

quarterly_data.signal: SCALE-ACROSS / DCI AND THE 7800R4: in Q4 2025 Arista launched the flat 7800R4 spine for routing use cases including DCI and AI spine, 'with that massive 460 terabytes of capacity'. CEO Jayshree Ullal: Arista expected its participation to be mostly scale out, but workloads too large for one data center (power, bandwidth, throughput) are being extended across data centers through fiber and very high injection bandwidth DCI routing; Arista is 'pleasantly surprised with the role of coherent long-haul optics, which we do not build', and the companies that build them 'are seeing the lift'. The 7800 spine chassis is the flagship there - 'a full-on Arista flagship box with EOS and all of the virtual output queuing and buffering' - interconnecting regional centers as a 'universal AI spine'.
quarterly_data.figure: 7800R4 spine; 460 terabytes of capacity

quarterly_data.signal: SCALE-UP TIMING (point-in-time; later calls pushed revenue out): CEO Jayshree Ullal said today's configurations are mostly a combination of scale out and scale up on 800 gig and smaller radix. Arista ties its scale-up commitment to new products and the ESUN specification, 'which we expect the earliest to be Q4 this year' - without a solid spec 'we will be shipping proprietary products like some people in the world do today'. Arista will be in trials on active AI racks designed with scale up in mind, 'But the real production level will be in 2027. Primarily centered around not just 800 gig, but 1.6T.'
quarterly_data.figure: ESUN spec earliest to be Q4 this year; real production level will be in 2027

quarterly_data.signal: Supply, not demand, is the binding constraint: the industry needs to add significant capacity and management does not see supply and demand getting back into balance BEFORE 2028 — a similarly constrained dynamic is expected going into 2027 and likely into 2028. In recent weeks Ciena FINALIZED LONG-TERM AGREEMENTS that secure supply of certain key components THROUGH 2029, including incremental capacity for those key components; the June five-year zero-coupon convertible (economic conversion premium of 114%, proceeds retiring the 5.5% interest term loan) partly provided the capital to help secure supply over the next three years, and cash from operations will step down in Q4 as those investments are dispersed. Ciena is also qualifying additional suppliers — expanding both the number of suppliers and alternative technologies for the same functionality. Capital investments this year increased capacity sufficient to support RLS, plug and Waveserver revenue growth all over 60% year to date; capex expected at the high end of the $250 million-$275 million range; $2.8 billion in cash and equivalents. Value exchange with customers: price increases from high single digits up to high teens/low 20s depending on customer and product line, some of it selectively hitting backlog, alongside payment-terms and fill-rate discussions; possible new Canadian tariff impact of ~$10 million a quarter being mitigated.
quarterly_data.figure: Key-component supply secured through 2029; supply/demand balance not before 2028; price increases high single digits to high teens/low 20s; capex high end of $250M-$275M

quarterly_data.signal: AI portfolio catalysts: WaveLogic 6 Extreme — after 18 months still the ONLY 1.6 Tb high-performance modem on the market — with a ramp already exceeding WaveLogic 5 Extreme and output doubled. RLS holds roughly 70% market share in disaggregated optical line systems; next-generation RLS HYPER-RAIL (co-created with the hyperscalers for scale-across / distributed AI training over greater distances) is on track for initial customer standardization by the end of calendar 2026 and will ramp to SEVERAL HUNDRED MILLION DOLLARS of revenue in 2027 (could be faster with more components), with economics a step function above RLS and accretive to corporate average margins. Interconnects: Q3 800 ZR pluggable shipments MORE THAN TWICE the previous quarter's volume; strong market receptivity to Nitro, the linear redriver for active copper cable solutions; VESTA, the open co-packaged optics (CPX) solution, received SAMPLE ORDERS FROM SEVERAL ANCHOR CUSTOMERS in the ecosystem — CPX revenue expected to begin in 2027 and ramp into 2028. Coherent moving inside the data center is viewed as inevitable with the right general-market intercept at 3.2 Tb; OCS is welcomed as driving coherent adoption inside the data center faster (no comment on Ciena entering the OCS market itself). The major-hyperscaler WaveLogic 6 Extreme win announced last quarter — DSP, drivers, TIAs and coherent expertise in a complete module deployed across the customer's own global optical platform, a significant takeaway from a component competitor — is one of two bespoke performance-optics consumption-model relationships. TAM expected to effectively double from approximately $25 billion today to approximately $50 billion by 2029; scale-across is a major demand driver, almost entirely North American/US-based and just beginning, with asynchronous training and inference traffic still ahead.

On NEW builds, CFO Stansbury was blunt: 'if you look at the cost to build new trenches, deploy new conduit, you're looking at returns that are AT OR BELOW COST OF CAPITAL levels... there's great headline generating news in those, but the RETURNS ARE TERRIBLE'. Lumen's answer is to ride others' fiber: 'we're quite happy for others to build at or below their cost of capital so that we can provision higher margin, higher growth services on top of them.' quarterly_data.signal: CALL-ONLY: NEOCLOUDS ARE 'GOING LONG' IN 100G/400G WAVES - THE CLEAREST CARRIER-SIDE AI SIGNAL IN THE QUARTER. Strategic WAVES revenue (100G and 400G) grew nearly 11% YoY in North American enterprise, and strategic WAVES SALES were up nearly 35% YoY - management called the sales number 'a nice precursor to future revenue'. CEO Johnson attributed it to share gain, not market growth: 'the neo clouds go long in 100 and 400 gig'... 'Yes, we're taking share', enabled by RAPIDROUTES turning up circuits 'in days, versus what used to take months' and by the density of '58 million fiber miles'. Neocloud PCF deals are 'relatively small' - neoclouds are buying WAVES, not conduit ('That is a part of the Waves growth... that's how they're choosing to buy their net connectivity'). Framing of the cycle: the uptick in 100G/400G 'is indicative of the SECOND PHASE OF THE AI ADOPTION CURVE, where more customers are starting to realize that they've got to upgrade their capacity', while legacy low-bandwidth wave circuits decline. Separately, satellite backhaul is a growing fiber-demand source - 'data needs to find fiber as fast as possible. We do the backhaul for the satellite companies and it's growing pretty significantly'.

Total business revenue $2.44B (-1.8% YoY); North American enterprise (ex-wholesale) down only 0.2%; STRATEGIC revenue +14% YoY (+23% on a two-year stack) and now 53% of business revenue, up from 51% in Q1 and 45% a year ago, while legacy fell ~15% - 'the mix shift... is happening faster than we expected'. Adjusted EBITDA (ex-special items) $802M vs ~$877M a year ago (mostly the fiber-to-the-home sale plus expected revenue declines); capex ex-special ~$780M; FCF ex-special $327M; special items $204M. Digital revenue $39M (from $37M). NaaS: total customers now EXCEED 3,000, new-customer adoption +22% QoQ with MORE THAN 20% brand new to Lumen (and ~60% of existing adopters ADDING circuits rather than migrating - 'clearly a share take, not a one for one translation'), active ports +34% QoQ and active services +29% QoQ - all in a north-south connectivity market 'growing less than 1% per year'. The margin thesis: DIA ports are being made digitally discoverable so incremental digital services (Lumen Defender, DDoS, Multi-Cloud Gateway) can be layered on without a truck roll, and those incremental services 'are expected to approach 80% ADJUSTED EBITDA MARGINS'. ALKIRA closed in early July (not in the Investor Day targets; revenue immaterial today, positioned as upside) - a cloud-native east-west multi-cloud/AI fabric, ~4,000 Lumen employees already trained, most platform integration targeted within 18 months; proof points cited: Koch Industries multi-cloud hub setup compressed from 8 months to 1 day, Michaels connected 1,400+ retail sites to Google Cloud in weeks with no capex. Portfolio pruning: enterprise voice/communications products moved to END OF SALE (low-single-digit % of sales) alongside the copper exit; modernization/simplification savings on track for $700M exiting 2026 and $1B exiting 2027.

quarterly_data.signal: Initial fiscal 2027 outlook: total revenue $6,850,000,000 to $7,150,000,000 (approximately 23.6% to 29% growth, 6.6% to 10.3% organic); Communications $5,700,000,000 to $5,900,000,000 with modest adjusted EBITDA margin gains; Building Systems $1,150,000,000 to $1,250,000,000 at a mid-teens adjusted EBITDA margin. Drivers: strong fiber-to-the-home demand, increasing long-haul and middle-mile fiber builds, growing inside-the-fence opportunities, modest service/maintenance growth, 'exceptional demand for electrical services in a growing data center market'; wireless equipment replacement revenue to decline by approximately $100,000,000 with a further step down in fiscal 2028. Long-haul / middle-mile / inside-the-fence data-center fiber: 'Existing networks lack the capacity and latency required to support growing data consumption and AI inference'; hyperscalers collectively raised capex guidance to nearly $718,000,000,000 (approximate 70% increase year-over-year). The $20,000,000,000 addressable market 'continues to grow' and the CEO 'strongly' believes it is more than that; it is back-half weighted, ramping this year and in 2027, with builds starting in earnest in calendar 2028. 'we are getting more phone calls and seeing more opportunities than we saw even a quarter ago or, frankly, even a week ago'. Dycom continues to secure new inside-the-fence awards; near-term hyperscale revenue is led by the Lumen overpull program plus shorter 100 or 200 mile routes, while routes of thousands of miles come later.

quarterly_data.signal: DATA CENTER IS NOW ~50% OF NSE REVENUE - AND IT IS ALL OPTICAL. CEO Khaykin sized the segments for the first time this precisely: data center ~50% of NSE, aerospace & defense ~17%, the rest service provider. 'Pretty much when we talk about data center, it's all optical' - optical in R&D/lab, optical for PRODUCTION test, optical for fiber monitoring and build-out - 'there's very little copper or anything, if anything at all'. The data-center business MORE THAN DOUBLED YoY EXCLUDING SPIRENT, and the fastest-growing piece is production test: 'everything from making fiber optic modules to making fiber optic cables to now getting into the CPO testing, where we're entering the TRADITIONAL SEMICONDUCTOR TEST. We play the OPTICAL PLANE of the semiconductor test, and that's a completely new market.' Product proof point: Viavi launched 'the industry's first validation solution for ULTRA ETHERNET TRANSPORT, purpose-built to support large-scale AI and high-performance computing workloads' (ahead of schedule on the Spirent roadmap integration; Spirent synergies/restructuring complete as of the June quarter, and Spirent revenue is guided +~10% QoQ into September with December its strongest quarter). Capex read-through offered by the CEO: 'if you tell me somebody's spent this year $600 billion and next year they're going to spend $1 trillion, I should expect at least that kind of growth... on this particular product lines, we should do BETTER than the purely CapEx growth' because 1.6T brings insertions where Viavi is 'not even present' today. A&D growth is driven by PNT (positioning, navigation, timing), called a multi-year driver; service provider is up on fiber monitoring for build-outs and cable DAA migration, while wireless stays 'anemic, although stable'.
quarterly_data.figure: Data center ~50% of NSE (A&D ~17%); DC business >2x YoY ex-Spirent; first Ultra Ethernet Transport validation solution

quarterly_data.signal: SPEED-NODE, CPO AND OCS ROADMAP FROM THE TEST SEAT. SPEED MIX: '800 Gbps is still the biggest driver, but 1.6 Tbps is ramping very quickly, and that's mainly a lot of the production' - management expects 'probably in 2027 it may get to PARITY between 800 Gbps and 1.6 Tbps, and then 1.6 Tbps will continue to get bigger while 800 Gbps may pull back'; 400G 'is going to be around for quite a while as well. They just don't go away' - multiple nodes running in parallel. CPO: asked about yield-driven slippage, Khaykin was emphatic - 'there's been a lot of industry talk, like, oh, because the yield is going to be slower. That's all NONSENSE. CPO and all that thing is MOVING FORWARD... I have POs to show for that.' Viavi is already recognizing some CPO revenue in the September quarter with December 'starting to accelerate'. Crucially, yield management INCREASES test intensity: 'to manage yields, you just do more tests - more of a KNOWN GOOD DIE, KNOWN GOOD OPTICAL ENGINE, KNOWN GOOD SUBSTRATE... which means a lot of testing, which ultimately pretty good for us.' And the cleanest statement yet of why CPO happens at all: 'if you have co-packaged optics, your THREE NANOMETER SILICON PERFORMS AS A TWO NANOMETER SILICON. You are getting almost a WHOLE NODE OF ADVANTAGE by co-packaging the optics' - taken either as performance or as cost, at the price of complexity and yield. OCS: some revenue already in the numbers with 'the majority... coming in the next several quarters'; Viavi has been selling equipment to 'a big OCS vendor, hyperscaler, who makes their own stuff', and it is now broadening as 'many other companies are looking to do more optical switching in their core' - 'I see this demand as being very healthy.'
quarterly_data.figure: 800G/1.6T parity ~2027 then 1.6T leads; CPO revenue starts Sept qtr, accelerates Dec; CPO = ~one node of silicon advantage
