quarterly_data.signal: 1.6T TEST ECONOMICS THE CALL DID NOT SIZE: CEO Oleg Khaykin said a 1.6T tester carries 'about 50% price increase' over an 800G box, 'because the components are much more expensive', comparing it to TSMC raising price per wafer 'about 1.5x' each node. Viavi has sold 1.6T equipment 'for over a year, mainly to the developers' (system, module and silicon vendors); production started 'beginning of this year' and adoption is 'maybe third inning for 1.6T, second, third inning, depending on who you are talking to'. The box is backward compatible - one 1.6T tester can test four 400G modules, two 800G or a 1.6T - so cost per bit falls even though cost per box rises, and one high-performance tester can service multiple production lines at once. Content per test is also rising: 400G was laser/dispersion/power in-out, 800G adds precise laser and insertion-loss measurement, and 'as you go to 1.6T, it is a whole new ballgame... a lot more functional test on the line'. On share, of the top 5 transceiver manufacturers Viavi works with all of them, engagement is 'very high with probably 4 out of 5', and with numbers 1, 2 and 3 'we are very much in all of their labs'.
quarterly_data.figure: 1.6T tester about 50% price increase versus 800G (TSMC node analogy about 1.5x); engagement very high with 4 out of 5 of the top 5 transceiver makers

quarterly_data.signal: CPO TEST - TIMING AND WHERE VIAVI SITS: Khaykin said Viavi has been working on a CPO test 'now for well over 12 to close to 2 years. We are now started shipping, I would say even this quarter is early shipments.' Test capacity is facilitized ahead of demand and the next increment is added at about '60%, 70% utilization'. CPO pulls Viavi into semiconductor test next to Advantest, Teradyne and FormFactor - the configuration is an IC tester plus a prober plus an optical rack, all interconnected - and he expects a HIGHER share for Viavi there than in pluggables because Viavi sells an automatable integrated platform with '2,500 SKUs' of measurement modules rather than a point solution. Content per port rises sharply: pluggable is power, dispersion and insertion loss, CPO is multiple insertions plus extensive functional test, with known-good-die, optical-engine and interconnect-platform insertions all before the ASIC and memory go on a module worth 'thousands of dollars' - skip them and 'you will be throwing away tens of millions of dollars'.
quarterly_data.figure: CPO test in development well over 12 months to close to 2 years, early shipments this quarter; capacity increments added at 60%, 70% utilization; 2,500 SKUs of measurement modules

quarterly_data.signal: OCS TEST ATTACH RATE QUANTIFIED: Khaykin said some players build in-house equipment but 'anybody who is buying merchant equipment, we are the dominant supplier' for optical circuit switch test. Asked how to convert an OCS TAM into a test opportunity, he said 'depending on the complexity, you'd say 10% of the annual size is what the test and measurement market ought to be' - that figure applies to the higher-end products such as OCS and CPO, and is 'a lower number for transceiver'. He noted OCS demand is not only from module vendors: 'there's also some hyperscalers who do it directly'. The driver is power - 'there's not enough power in the world to power all these data centers' - pushing architectures from electrical to optical. Because the cost of one bad port pair is a bad switch, customers 'test everything to the nth degree', and for a '100 terabit switch, I don't think anybody's going to skip any tests'.
quarterly_data.figure: test and measurement should be about 10% of the annual size of the high-end (OCS, CPO) market, lower for transceivers

quarterly_data.signal: FIELD INSTRUMENTS ARE NOW A DATA-CENTER BUSINESS: Khaykin called it 'one big surprise for us' - the traditional field instrument line is 'today, that business is over 40% data center driven', led by advanced fiber monitoring. Hyperscalers that bought a lot of dark fiber found 'sometimes the fiber worked... but when you turn it on, you find it does not work', so they now put fiber monitoring at the edge and test, qualify and monitor every fiber across the whole build-out, then pick the best-performing fiber when they turn up capacity, using the collected parametrics to predict outages. 'If you ask me who is the state-of-the-art fiber operator today, it would be the hyperscalers.'
quarterly_data.figure: field instrument business over 40% data center driven

quarterly_data.signal: $500M RUN RATE AND, NEW, THE MARGIN AT THAT LEVEL: Khaykin said Viavi will be 'probably not far from $500 million in the December quarter. If demand strengthens up, heck, we may even hit it... we could get very close within the whisker, even this December quarter' - against a fiscal 2028 framing given three months earlier, which GC Ilan Daskal confirmed had already been pulled in on the last call. New here is profitability at that run rate: asked whether a 30% operating margin is in the model at $500 million, Daskal said 'the high 40 is not an unrealistic number to get to when we get to the 500. That is not an unrealistic thinking.' Khaykin added that incremental dollars carry a near-zero tax rate (U.S. jurisdiction plus the NOLs kept from the Lumentum separation, most converted into amortizable assets) and lower interest after the term-loan payoff, so operating leverage is amplified again at the net line.
quarterly_data.figure: $500 million quarterly revenue possible as early as the December quarter; high 40 operating margin when Viavi reaches the 500

quarterly_data.signal: A NEW FIBER-CONNECTOR TEST MARKET AND THE TUCK-IN THAT SERVES IT: Khaykin said hollow-core, multi-core and multi-ribbon cables plugged in '8, 16, 32' at a time are 'opening all new markets now in manufacturing for fiber' - if one fiber in an expensive connector is bad the whole connector is thrown away, so customers now use interferometry on surface quality because at these speeds 'any kind of imperfection can impact the quality of service'. Viavi 'just bought this company called Digital Optical Research Corp, or for short, DORC', an interferometry specialist, and he said that once it is put into Viavi's production test 'it will go from couple million to tens of millions of dollars'. On M&A discipline he said Viavi walked away from a deal announced that day where 'The price paid was 2x more than what we were prepared to pay'.
quarterly_data.figure: hollow-core, multi-core and multi-ribbon connectors of 8, 16, 32 fibers; DORC interferometry to go from couple million to tens of millions of dollars in Viavi production test

quarterly_data.signal: SCALE-ACROSS SITS INSIDE VIAVI'S DATA CENTER REVENUE: CEO Oleg Khaykin clarified the definition - 'if we’re selling to a tier 2 player like say Lumen or Zayo, who are interconnecting all those data centers, right? We count it as a data center revenue' - because 'it’s who pays for all that equipment'; 'If Verizon sells to data centers, we’ll count their revenue as a scale-across.' Service provider means traditional metro, fiber to the home and wireless carriers, growing low single digits. When the moderator asked whether sales to OEMs such as Ciena, Nokia or Cisco for a hyperscaler application are also included, Khaykin answered 'It counts as a data center. Exactly.' (The roughly 50% data-center share of NSE was the moderator's recap, not restated by management here.)
quarterly_data.figure: no specific figure

quarterly_data.signal: FISCAL Q2 2026 (DECEMBER QUARTER) RESULTS - HIGH END OF GUIDANCE. CFO Ilan Daskal: 'Net revenue for the quarter was $369.3 million, which is at the high end of our guidance range of $360 million and $370 million. Revenue was up 23.5% sequentially and on a year-over-year basis, was up 36.4%.' Operating margin was 19.3%, above the high end of the 17.3% to 18.5% guide (up 360 basis points QoQ and 440 basis points YoY), and EPS was $0.22, above the $0.18 to $0.20 guide. OSP revenue was $77.8 million, up 9.7% YoY, on strength in anti-counterfeiting; 3D sensing demand was in line with seasonal expectations. CapEx for the quarter was $5.6 million.
quarterly_data.figure: revenue $369.3 million (up 23.5% sequentially, up 36.4% YoY); operating margin 19.3%; EPS $0.22; OSP $77.8 million (up 9.7%)

quarterly_data.signal: NSE SEGMENT - DATA CENTER ECOSYSTEM IS THE DRIVER, SPIRENT SLIGHTLY LIGHT. NSE revenue was $291.5 million (high end of the $283 million to $293 million guide), up 45.8% YoY on the Inertia Labs and Spirent product-line acquisitions plus 'strong demand for lead and production and field products driven by the data center ecosystem'; NSE operating margin 15.6% vs 8.7% a year ago. 'Revenue from Spirent was $43 million, which was slightly below our expectation of $45 million to $55 million due to timing of certain opportunities.' CEO Oleg Khaykin: the data center ecosystem, 'which includes high-performance semis, optical modules, and NAMS, drove strong demand for lead and production products in support of AI data center build-out', and Viavi is 'now also seeing emerging strong demand for our fiber field instruments by hyperscalers and service providers' to build next-generation fiber networks that interconnect data centers. Aerospace and defense grew again on positioning, navigation, and timing products; service providers were 'generally stable'; wireless infrastructure test 'continues to be weak but stable'.
quarterly_data.figure: NSE revenue $291.5 million (up 45.8% YoY); NSE operating margin 15.6%; Spirent revenue $43 million vs $45 million to $55 million expected

quarterly_data.signal: FISCAL Q3 2026 (MARCH QUARTER) GUIDANCE - UP SEQUENTIALLY IN A SEASONALLY WEAK QUARTER. CFO: 'we expect Viavi revenue in the range of $386 million and $400 million. We expect total NSE revenue between $304 million and $316 million. OSP revenue is expected to be in the range of $82 million and $84 million.' NSE growth driven by 'continued strong demand for lead and production and field products, which is driven by the data center ecosystem as well as aerospace and defense customers', and the guide includes a full thirteen weeks of Spirent product lines versus ten weeks in the December quarter. quarterly_data.figure: FQ3 revenue $386 million to $400 million; NSE $304 million to $316 million; OSP $82 million to $84 million; operating margin 19.7% plus or minus 50 basis points

quarterly_data.signal: MIX FLIPPED TO DATA CENTER; VISIBILITY STRETCHED. Khaykin: 'last quarter, we kinda talked 45% service provider, 40% data center, 15% aerospace and defense', and now 'closer the other way around 40% service provider, 45% data center, around 15% aerospace and defense' - service provider trending 'a little bit below 40%', not because it is shrinking ('Actually, steady and showing slight recovery') but because growth rates differ; 'I'd say 60% is driven by the data center ecosystem and the aerospace and defense.' On data center visibility: 'traditionally, we only have, like, maybe one, one and a half quarter visibility. We we we have a pretty good view, at least on the base demand from this type of activities up to three quarters ahead.'
quarterly_data.figure: mix now about 45% data center, a little below 40% service provider, around 15% aerospace and defense (vs 45% service provider, 40% data center last quarter); data center base-demand view up to three quarters ahead (traditionally maybe one, one and a half quarter visibility)

quarterly_data.signal: FIELD INSTRUMENTS TURN INTO A DATA-CENTER BUSINESS. Khaykin: 'if I looked at a year ago, you might have been single digits data center for our traditional field instruments. I think we are now looking at about a third of our revenue in the field instruments coming out from data center.' Buyers are 'next gen service providers' interconnecting data centers and 'the data center operators themselves investing into our fiber monitoring and fiber measurement systems'; 'we are seeing a lot of pressure from the hyperscalers on service providers to improve the performance', and hyperscalers put 'monitoring and policing' on their networks. At AI data centers 'they want to monitor every incoming you know, wavelength' against service level agreements with the service providers, and he expects service providers to follow the hyperscalers with a lag of 'maybe by a couple quarters'.
quarterly_data.figure: about a third of field instrument revenue from data center (vs single digits a year ago)

quarterly_data.signal: PRODUCTION TEST IS THE FASTER GROWER; REPURPOSED PRODUCTION CAPACITY IS A FRACTION OF WHAT IS NEEDED. Khaykin: lab instruments track 'the r and d CapEx at semis system vendors, and module vendors', production test is 'heavily driven by volume' ('for every tranche of volume, you need to increase capacity'), and field instruments are linked to the number of data centers being built - the higher growth is 'clearly clearly gonna be the production'. On the cycle: 'pretty much every ounce of capacity that was kinda abandoned by service providers when they cut back about three years ago in investment. It's been totally repurposed into the data center. And it's a fraction of what they need', so 'you're gonna see significant growth over the next two years'. Node cadence has compressed: 'We now see the new each technology notes turning over. Every two years. So no longer, let's say, between between a 100 gig and a 400 gig you have six years. You really now have two years between'.
quarterly_data.figure: technology nodes turning over every two years (vs six years between a 100 gig and a 400 gig); significant growth over the next two years

quarterly_data.signal: WHO BUYS THE OPTICAL TEST AND WHAT IS NEW. Khaykin: 'every segment, we see growing' - semiconductor and memory vendors, a 'dozen so companies in Asia making pluggables and, of course, the big leaders in North America for cross points, which is optical switches', module makers and the NAMS supplying equipment into data centers (no company named). Lab demand is 'Heavily driven' by 'everything to do with 1.6 and PCI Express six point o'; production test runs from passive and active components to the final product, now 'including testing fiber as you we're now seeing emergence of hollow core fiber and multiport fiber And this is a whole new thing'. Management groups all of it as the 'data center ecosystem', 'which includes semis, modules, systems, and field instruments that are used in data centers themselves'.
quarterly_data.figure: no specific figure

quarterly_data.signal: TIMING PRODUCTS: FROM DRONES TO HIGHER-SPEED DATA CENTERS. Khaykin: the biggest aerospace and defense driver is 'resilient PNT' for operating without a GPS signal - 'it's drones, drones, and more drones' across autonomous systems. The PNT timing line also sees 'emerging opportunities in data centers' because 'as you increase the speeds in the data centers, you need accurate timing for synchronization': a traditional distributed clock 'may be fine when you're a 100 gig data center when you're going to one point six three point two. The latency becomes unbearable. So we are looking we're seeing demand for timing'.
quarterly_data.figure: no specific figure

quarterly_data.signal: WHY THE MARCH QUARTER IS UP DESPITE SEASONALITY. Khaykin: in the old Viavi 'service providers were over 80% of NSC' and did not release budgets until February, so the March quarter was weak; now 'the strength in the data center, aerospace defense, and also, the sparring business is not only offsetting, it's actually more than offsetting. That's why the net net, the quarter is gonna be up for NSE.' ('sparring' is the transcript's rendering of Spirent) For Spirent, some government orders slipped from the December quarter into the March quarter ('Between the shutdown and, of course, you know, this one time grant to the government employees of Christmas holidays'), so 'we expect March quarter relatively to be stronger for them'. Cable operators show 'some opportunistic demand' as they transition to the new DAA architecture and access 4.0 standard.
quarterly_data.figure: service providers were over 80% of NSE in the old Viavi (no specific figure for the quarter)

quarterly_data.signal: RESTRUCTURING TO FUND DATA CENTER AND DEFENSE; DEBT PAYDOWN. CFO: a restructuring plan will affect 'approximately 5% of our global workforce' with 'approximately $32 million restructuring charges', for 'annual savings of about $30 million' (including the previously communicated $16 million of Spirent synergies); majority of charges by June 2026, substantially complete by December 2026. Khaykin: cost comes 'out of the slower or stagnant, product segments' to put more 'wood behind the arrow on things like data center ecosystem, aerospace and defense'. Balance sheet: cash and short-term investments $772.1 million; about $100 million of 1.625% convertible notes exchanged for 7.9 million shares; $100 million of the $600 million term loan B prepaid in January 2026; no buybacks in the quarter; an Inertia Labs earn-out of about $75 million to be paid during the third fiscal quarter ('as a result of their strong performance in calendar 2025').
quarterly_data.figure: approximately 5% of workforce; approximately $32 million charges; annual savings of about $30 million; $100 million of the $600 million term loan B prepaid; Inertia Labs earn-out about $75 million

quarterly_data.signal: OPTICAL IS NOW AEHR'S SECOND PILLAR: optical device test and burn-in for DATA CENTER INFRASTRUCTURE TRANSCEIVERS, CHIP-TO-CHIP I/O and hard disk drives accounted for approximately 20% OF FISCAL 2026 REVENUE, alongside AI accelerators/CPUs/network processors at ~71% — and management expects BOTH markets to grow significantly in fiscal 2027. Silicon photonics is named as one of the two focus areas (with AI accelerators) that together drove the majority of fourth-quarter revenue. quarterly_data.signal: AI test intensity is compounding because design margins are shrinking: higher data rates, lower latency and the requirement that AI fabrics be LOSSLESS mean customers 'can no longer guarantee anything by design' and must test in production too. A compute or switch tray has gone from tens to HUNDREDS of IC pinouts - more insertion points - tested at signal level (VNAs, oscilloscopes), at bit level (new portfolio) and at protocol/packet level (AI workload emulators). The move from monolithic chips to CHIPLET architectures adds interoperability emulation, and customers now ask for emulation environments that stress a chip while it exercises a model (thermal shutdown, all cores active at higher power and speed). The ecosystem is shifting from a homogeneous integrated vertical stack to a HETEROGENEOUS one - GPU/CPU/DPU mixes and a growing number of protocols at every layer of the stack - which broadens Keysight's addressable tail. The four wireline pillars (AI infrastructure scaling, speed transitions, silicon photonics, system-level emulation) all drove growth. Hyperscaler engagement (rooted in the Ixia acquisition ~5 years ago) is deepening as they integrate Keysight pre-silicon emulation and workload solutions into their development pipelines; hyperscalers plus the model companies are ~10% OF REVENUE DIRECTLY but drive large downstream influence, and many are building their own in-house silicon. Switch designers use Keysight emulators to validate network performance across AI workloads and protocols; interconnect manufacturers use high-fidelity analyzers to characterize high-speed backplanes for signal integrity and manufacturing yield.

contracts.signal: AXT announced a strategic long-term supply agreement with LUMENTUM in the week of the Q2 call, following similar agreements with Coherent and one other partner. AXT frames these LTAs as confirmation that its InP capacity build-out is 'mirrored and necessary' against customer road maps.

Lumentum confirmed the AXT indium phosphide substrate deal from the buyer side, signed during its fiscal Q4 (quarter ended 06-27-2026). Trigger was a surge in ultra-high-power (CPO/NPO) laser demand across a couple of customers that outran Lumentum's existing substrate arrangements: 'we have seen a pretty big surge in demand... in order to respond to that, we went out and we found additional substrate help from AXT.' Lumentum expects it may need still more substrate supply if the demand vector continues.

On July 26, 2026 AXT and Lumentum Operations LLC entered a Capacity Reservation Agreement for the supply and capacity reservation of indium phosphide wafer substrates: AXT reserves a minimum annual commitment of the products for Lumentum for a six-year period (the press release says through December 31, 2031) and will support additional capacity if required. Lumentum pays an initial deposit of $43,500,000 within thirty business days and a second deposit of $43,500,000 with timing and terms to be determined during calendar year 2028; the deposits are applied as shipment credits, and Lumentum is responsible for any shortfall below its annual purchase commitment.
